docs.title: Spark Connect Rust Client
docs.text:
A fast, native Rust client for Apache Spark Connect - and a drop-in pyspark replacement.

It builds spark.connect protobuf plans, manages the gRPC channel, and decodes Arrow results in Rust - speaking the same protocol and returning the same results as the reference client.

Get started Quickstart View on GitHub

Coming from Python?

pyspark-client-rust is a faster, drop-in replacement for the pyspark-client package on PyPI. Uninstall any existing pyspark / pyspark-client, pip install pyspark-client-rust, and your Spark Connect code runs unchanged - same imports, same API, same server (see Installation). Use it exactly like PySpark; the rest of these docs cover the native Rust API. New to the different pyspark packages on PyPI? See Which client am I using?.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: The reference Spark Connect client is pure Python - it builds protobuf plans, manages the gRPC channel, and decodes Arrow results in Python. This project moves that work into Rust: a synchronous, PySpark-shaped DataFrame API you can use directly from Rust, and - through PyO3 - a byte-for-byte compatible pyspark package for the Python world.

docs.title: Native Rust API
docs.text: A synchronous spark_connect crate that mirrors PySpark's DataFrame, Column, functions, SQL, streaming, and catalog surface.

docs.title: Same protocol & results
docs.text: Speaks the same spark.connect gRPC/protobuf protocol against the same server, validated against the official Apache Spark test suite.

docs.title: Hello, Spark Connect (in Rust)
docs.text:
use spark_connect::{SparkSession, functions as f, lit};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let spark = SparkSession::builder()
        .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
        .get_or_create()?;

    let df = spark
        .range(1_000_000)?
        .select([(f::col("id") * lit(2)).alias("x")])
        .filter((f::col("x") % lit(3)).eq(lit(0)));

    println!("count = {}", df.count()?);
    df.show(20)?;
    Ok(())
}

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: One protocol, one Rust core, two front-ends. This project reimplements the Spark Connect client - plan building, gRPC transport, and Arrow result decoding - in Rust, and exposes it both as a native Rust library and, through PyO3, as a drop-in pyspark package.

docs.title: The one big idea
docs.text:
A Spark Connect client does three things: it builds a protobuf plan from your DataFrame/SQL operations, sends it over gRPC to a Spark Connect server, and decodes the Arrow result the server streams back. The reference client does all three in Python.

Here, those three jobs live in Rust crates. On top of that core sit two thin front-ends that share it: a synchronous Rust API shaped like PySpark, and a pyspark Python package (a PyO3 extension) that is byte-for-byte compatible with the reference client. Same spark.connect protocol, same server, same results.

docs.title: A query's lifecycle
docs.text:
When you call an action such as count() or show(), the lazily-built plan is serialized and sent to the server; results stream back as Arrow batches.

Day-time intervals use signed 64-bit microseconds in Rust (Value::DayTimeInterval) and Python datetime.timedelta values. createDataFrame supports inferred and explicit interval schemas, including nested structs, lists, maps, and nulls. Collected rows can be passed back with their schema. As in PySpark, an int or a float for an interval field is taken as microseconds, and a value outside the signed 64-bit microsecond range is an error.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Your code (Rust or pyspark)
    participant API as spark-connect
    participant Core as spark-connect-core
    participant Srv as Spark Connect server

    App->>API: range(...).select(...).filter(...)
    Note over API: builds a spark.connect Plan (lazy)
    App->>API: count() / show()  (action)
    API->>Core: execute(plan)
    Core->>Srv: ExecutePlan(plan)  [gRPC/HTTP2]
    Srv-->>Core: ExecutePlanResponse* (Arrow IPC batches)
    Note over Core,Srv: ReattachExecute resumes a broken stream
    Core->>API: decoded Arrow batches
    API-->>App: rows / count / DataFrame

Transformations are lazy - they only build up the plan. Only an action triggers ExecutePlan. If the response stream breaks mid-flight, or the server ends it before the result is complete (as it does after spark.connect.execute.reattachable.senderMaxStreamDuration or senderMaxStreamSize), the core's reattachable-execute iterator resumes from the last response it saw, so long results survive transient disconnects. Like the reference client, it releases each response it has read, and the whole execution once the result is complete, so the server does not keep them.

spark.sql() is the exception, as in the reference client: it sends the statement at once. A command such as CREATE VIEW or SET takes effect there, and its DataFrame holds the result the server returned; a statement that does not parse or resolve fails there. A query's DataFrame still runs at an action.

Each plan node gets its plan ID once, the first time it is sent, and keeps it, as in the reference client. Re-executing a DataFrame therefore sends the same relation, and a DataFrame built on another keeps that input's plan IDs, so the server's per-session plan cache (spark.connect.session.planCache.*) can reuse the plans it already resolved instead of resolving them again. As with the reference client, a re-executed DataFrame can then use its earlier resolution. A DataFrame from spark.read.parquet(path), for example, keeps the file listing it resolved: once the files under path are overwritten, running it again fails with FAILED_READ_FILE.FILE_NOT_EXIST, while a new spark.read.parquet(path) reads the new files. Setting spark.connect.session.planCache.enabled to false turns the cache off, on the server or for a session with spark.conf.set.

docs.title: Python Arrow table handoff
docs.text:
toArrow() collects decoded batches and uses arrow-rs's IntoPyArrow for one boxed RecordBatchReader. Compatible value and offset buffers are shared; network decoding, sliced validity bitmaps, and pandas conversion may still copy. Batch schema consistency is validated before export. Field names or timezones containing NUL use IPC over the collected batches, without another RPC. Empty batch vectors retain the empty-schema behavior.

createDataFrame(pyarrow_table) uses the reverse boundary: Spark's schema and timestamp conversion helpers normalize the table, then arrow-rs imports its RecordBatchReader through the C Stream interface. The Rust core serializes those batches to IPC for the local relation sent to Spark. No Python rows are materialized; casts, buffer alignment, and IPC serialization may still copy. Empty tables require an explicit schema, matching PySpark Connect. Pandas inputs with only NumPy int64 or pandas nullable Int64 columns also use this importer, preserving integer precision and null masks without Python rows. Small frames (fewer than 1,000 rows) with only NumPy columns retain the row path to avoid the configuration RPC of the importer; nullable Int64 columns use Arrow at any size. This initial path accepts inferred schemas, complete string column names, and explicit StructType schemas whose fields are all LongType. Other dtypes, DDL/atomic schemas, schema conversions, NUL names, and duplicate/non-string input names retain the existing row conversion path. verifySchema remains ignored for pandas Arrow input, matching Spark Connect. Pandas frames of at least 100,000 rows whose columns are all NumPy float64, with an explicit StructType of DoubleType fields, are encoded to Arrow IPC from their columns, with pandas' missing values as nulls, and sent inline as the row path sends them, without the importer's configuration RPC. Pandas object columns containing exact datetime.date values or None use the Arrow importer at 10,000 rows or more with an explicit StructType of DateType fields. Unsupported values and customized inputs retain the row conversion path. Pandas frames of at least 10,000 rows whose columns are all kept in pandas' Arrow string storage (string[pyarrow] in pandas 2.2 and later, and the str dtype of pandas 3), with an explicit StructType of StringType fields, pass that storage to this importer as Arrow string columns, without Python rows. Inputs at or above spark.sql.session.localRelationCacheThreshold are serialized into independent IPC streams and uploaded as session-scoped cache artifacts. The plan carries ChunkedCachedLocalRelation hashes instead of embedding the entire payload. Spark infers omitted schemas from the Arrow streams; explicit schemas travel in the local relation or a separate schema artifact. Chunk sizes, upload batch sizes, and the total relation size limit follow the server's local-relation settings; artifact RPC messages use 32 KiB pieces, with SHA-256 deduplication and CRC checks.

Rust UDFs on the executors
docs.text:
Beyond the client, a Rust function can be compiled to WebAssembly and run as a Spark UDF on the executors - shipped inside a standard PythonUDF and executed with wasmtime, so nothing Rust-specific is needed server-side.

    WASM -->|"cloudpickled into a PythonUDF"| SRV["Spark executors"]
    SRV -->|"wasmtime runs it per batch or row"| RES["UDF result column"]

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
1. Don't fork PySpark's semantics - mirror the public API and match the reference client's protobuf output, verified by golden-proto tests.
  2. One core, thin front-ends - the Python package adds no client logic the Rust API doesn't already have.
  3. Correctness is gated in CI - golden-proto tests guard plan building; the official Apache Spark Connect test suite guards transport and Arrow paths (see the CI notes under dev/design/).
  4. Version = Spark version - the crate/wheel version tracks the Spark release it targets, so the number tells you which Spark it speaks.

For the deeper design write-ups (design notes, CI, the official test suite, and acceptance criteria), see dev/design/ in the repository.

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text: The Spark catalog provides metadata and management operations for databases, tables, columns, and functions.

docs.title: Accessing the Catalog
docs.text: let catalog = spark.catalog();

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
List, switch, and inspect databases:

// List all databases (returns a DataFrame)
let dbs = spark.catalog().list_databases()?;
dbs.show(20)?;

// Current database
let current = spark.catalog().current_database()?;

// Set current database
spark.catalog().set_current_database("my_db")?;

// Check existence
let exists = spark.catalog().database_exists("my_db")?;

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
List, inspect, and check tables:

// List tables in current database (returns a DataFrame)
let tables = spark.catalog().list_tables()?;
tables.show(20)?;

// List tables in specific database
let tables = spark.catalog().list_tables_in_database("my_db")?;

// Check existence
let exists = spark.catalog().table_exists("my_table")?;
let exists = spark.catalog().table_exists_with_database("my_table", Some("my_db"))?;

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
List columns in a table:

// List columns in current database (returns a DataFrame)
let cols = spark.catalog().list_columns("my_table")?;
cols.show(20)?;

// List columns in specific database
let cols = spark.catalog().list_columns_with_database("my_table", Some("my_db"))?;

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
List and check functions:

// List all functions (returns a DataFrame)
let funcs = spark.catalog().list_functions()?;
funcs.show(20)?;

// List functions in specific database
let funcs = spark.catalog().list_functions_in_database("my_db")?;

// Check existence
let exists = spark.catalog().function_exists("my_func")?;
let exists = spark.catalog().function_exists_with_database("my_func", Some("my_db"))?;

docs.title: Temporary Views
docs.text:
Register and drop temporary views (local to session):

// Register temp view
df.create_temp_view("my_view")?;

// Register and replace
df.create_or_replace_temp_view("my_view")?;

// Register global temp view (cross-session)
df.create_global_temp_view("my_global_view")?;

// Query temp view
let result = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM my_view")?;

// Drop temp view
spark.catalog().drop_temp_view("my_view")?;

// Drop global temp view
spark.catalog().drop_global_temp_view("my_global_view")?;

docs.title: Cache Management
docs.text:
Cache and uncache tables for performance:

// Cache table
spark.catalog().cache_table("my_table")?;

// Uncache table
spark.catalog().uncache_table("my_table")?;

// Clear all caches
spark.catalog().clear_cache()?;

Note

Temporary views are session-local and persist until the session ends. Global temporary views are prefixed with global_temp. by default.

docs.title: Columns and Functions
docs.text: Column expressions form the building blocks of transformations. Reference columns, build expressions with operators, and apply built-in functions from the spark_connect::functions module.

docs.title: Column References and Literals
docs.text:
Access DataFrame columns and create constant values.

use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit, lit_string};

// Column reference
let col_expr = f::col("column_name");

// Literal value
let lit_expr = lit(42);
let lit_expr = lit_string("hello");

// Use in expression
let df = df.filter(f::col("age").gt(lit(18)));

docs.title: Arithmetic & Comparison
docs.text:
use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit, lit_string};

// Arithmetic
let expr = f::col("x") + f::col("y");
let expr = f::col("x") - f::col("y");
let expr = f::col("x") * lit(2);
let expr = f::col("x") / lit(10);

// Comparison
let expr = f::col("age").gt(lit(18));
let expr = f::col("age").ge(lit(18));
let expr = f::col("salary").eq(lit(50000));
let expr = f::col("status").ne(lit_string("inactive"));

docs.title: Boolean Logic
docs.text:
use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit, lit_string, lit_boolean};

// AND
let expr = (f::col("age").gt(lit(18)))
    .and(f::col("city").eq(lit_string("NYC")));

// OR
let expr = (f::col("status").eq(lit_string("active")))
    .or(f::col("vip").eq(lit_boolean(true)));

// NOT
let expr = f::col("archived").eq(lit_boolean(true)).not();

docs.title: Aliasing, Casting, Null Handling
docs.text:
use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit_string};
use spark_connect::column::when; // CASE/WHEN builder (supports `.otherwise`)

// Alias
let expr = f::col("amount").alias("total");

// Cast to type
let expr = f::col("id").cast_str("string");
let expr = f::col("price").cast_str("decimal(10, 2)");

// Null checks
let expr = f::col("email").is_null();
let expr = f::col("email").is_not_null();

// Null fallback (coalesce-style) via when/otherwise
let expr = when(f::col("email").is_not_null(), f::col("email"))
    .otherwise(f::col("backup_email"));

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: This client aims for full API parity with the reference PySpark Spark Connect client (pyspark.sql.connect.*) and the shared modules it depends on. The goal is that existing Spark Connect code runs unchanged and gets byte-for-byte identical results. For how this client relates to the pyspark and pyspark-client packages on PyPI - and how to tell which one you have installed - see Which client am I using?.

docs.title: Supported Spark
docs.text: Apache Spark 4.3.0 and later. The crate and wheel version tracks the Spark release it targets (starting at 4.3.0), so the version number tells you which Spark it speaks.

docs.title: Rust migration for the 4.3 line
docs.text:
Value and LiteralExpression add a DayTimeInterval(i64) variant for signed microseconds. Downstream exhaustive matches on these public enums must handle the new variant. Rust interval map keys are stringified as raw microseconds; Python timedelta map keys are not yet supported.

DataFrame::sort, order_by, sort_within_partitions, agg, observe, observe_with, hint_expressions, repartition_by_range, repartition_by_range_opt, repartition_by_expressions, GroupedData::agg, the partition_by and order_by of Window and WindowSpec, and TableValuedFunction::udtf take impl IntoIterator<Item = impl Into<Column>>, as select and group_by do: Columns, column names or expressions, such as df.sort([col("x").desc()]) and .agg([sum(col("id")).alias("total")]), without .expression().clone(). So does the first list of drop_columns, of column references: a name in it is col(name), as in PySpark's drop(F.col(name)), so a name of several columns is AMBIGUOUS_REFERENCE, and a dotted name such as a.b refers to the field b of a column a, which drops nothing ("`a.b`" refers to a column named a.b). Its second list is of plain names, as that of drop: a name drops every column of that name, and a.b the column named a.b. grouping_sets takes any iterable of grouping sets, each any iterable of Columns, such as [[col("a")], [col("a"), col("b")]], and grouping_sets_with_columns takes such sets and any iterable of the grouping Columns. The names of drop, describe, to_df, to_schema, melt, the numeric aggregates of GroupedData (sum, avg, min, max, mean, numeric_agg), the freq_items and approx_quantile of StatFunctions, Column::drop_fields and the partition_by and cluster_by of DataStreamWriter take any iterable of names, as do the SQL expressions of select_expr, the statistics of summary and the paths of DataFrameReader::load_paths. The (name, Column) pairs of with_columns and the (old, new) pairs of with_columns_renamed take any iterable of pairs, and so do the (String, Value) pairs of fillna_map, such as a BTreeMap<String, Value> (its names stay Strings, so that vec![] and ("id".into(), value) still infer their type). functions::count_distinct_columns and UserDefinedFunction::to_expression (wasm) take any Columns. A Vec or an array of them compiles as before. The Vec<Expression> that the sort and aggregate methods took still compiles, by the new From<Expression> for Column, and so does the Vec<SortOrder> of the order_by of a window, by From<SortOrder> for Column; there a Column that is not a sort order is sorted ascending, nulls first, as PySpark's WindowSpec.orderBy sorts it. An empty vec![] or [] has no item type to infer: pass Vec::<Column>::new() or Vec::<&str>::new() instead. This breaks a caller of v4.2.0 that passes an empty literal to select_expr or summary, which took a Vec<&str> there: df.summary(vec![]), for the default statistics, becomes df.summary(Vec::<&str>::new()). load_paths is new in this release: v4.2.0 had only load, so no v4.2.0 caller breaks on it, and a new caller passes an empty literal as load_paths(Vec::<&str>::new()). The optional subset arguments of the null functions, the optional value_vars of melt and the optional column_names of drop_duplicates and drop_duplicates_within_watermark stay Option<Vec<&str>>, as in v4.2.0, so that None still infers its type. The optional values of unpivot takes any iterable, as in v4.2.0, so its None has no item type to infer, unlike that of melt: pass None::<Vec<Column>> or None::<[&str; 0]> to unpivot every column that is not an id.

BinaryClassificationEvaluator::set_score_col and score_col, and the Python scoreCol= argument and setScoreCol of v4.2.0 are removed, without an alias: Spark's evaluator has no scoreCol param, so no value of it worked on the server. Use set_raw_prediction_col and raw_prediction_col in Rust, and rawPredictionCol= / setRawPredictionCol in Python. They follow standard pyspark.ml.evaluation.BinaryClassificationEvaluator, whose default input column is rawPrediction and whose scores may be doubles or vectors.

The native ML classes take a JVM Int param as an i32: LogisticRegression::set_max_iter, LinearSVC::set_max_iter and LinearSVC::set_aggregation_depth take an i32, and LogisticRegression::max_iter returns one. Every native estimator has a getter of each of its params (KMeans::k, RandomForestClassifier::num_trees, ...), which reads its Params: the value that is set, else Spark's default (None for seed, weight_col and thresholds). The fields of LogisticRegressionModel, StringIndexerModel and MaxAbsScalerModel are private, as those of the other fitted models but PipelineModel: use Transformer::operator and Transformer::params, and LogisticRegressionModel::feature_col, label_col and prediction_col. VectorAssembler::input_cols and Pipeline::stages return a Vec<String>, and VectorAssembler::set_input_cols and Pipeline::set_stages take impl IntoIterator<Item = impl Into<String>>. The input_col of StandardScaler, MaxAbsScaler and StringIndexer returns an Option<&str>, which is None unless set: as in Spark, it has no default. Their output_col, and that of VectorAssembler, return a String, Spark's <uid>__output unless set, the column that the server writes. Before, they gave names that the server never wrote, such as scaled_features.

Params::set_param_int32, set_param_int_narrow, set_param_string_array and set_param_double_array are public, with the new Params::clear_param, and the evaluators have a params_mut, as estimators and transformers do. Seeds, CrossValidator::set_seed's included, are sent as the narrowest integer literal that holds them, as PySpark sends a Python int. MlOperator::new makes a uid of the simple class name and 12 hex digits (KMeans_1a2b3c4d5e6f), as PySpark and Spark do, instead of a bare UUID.

DataFrame::fillna_value and DataFrame::fillna_map return a Result, as dropna does. As PySpark's fillna, they take a bool, an integer, a float or a string (an integer is sent as a long, a float as a double), and reject other values with NOT_EXPECTED_TYPE and an empty map with CANNOT_BE_EMPTY. Before, such a value filled string columns with its debug text. A Value::Map given to fillna_value fills the columns of its keys, as PySpark's fillna of a dict, instead of being rejected. fillna, fillna_double, fillna_string and fillna_bool are unchanged.

A transport failure has the gRPC code that grpc-python gives it, which PySpark's errors and retries see. SparkError::grpc_code is UNAVAILABLE (14) for a connection that closes or is reset under a call, where it was UNKNOWN (2); for a call that its connection closes before sending it, where it was CANCELLED (1); and for a connection that the server ends with a GOAWAY, where it was the code of the reason of the GOAWAY, such as INTERNAL (13) for NO_ERROR and RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED (8) for ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM. It is INTERNAL (13) for a stream that the server resets with a reason that tonic leaves unmapped, such as STREAM_CLOSED, which is no longer retried.

The 4.3 line changes the public Rust representation of expressions and logical plans to share immutable nodes. This is a breaking change for code that directly constructs or matches these representations. The Column and DataFrame APIs, Python APIs, and Spark Connect protocol are unchanged by this representation change.

Expression is now a shared handle; its previous enum variants live in ExpressionNode. Construct an ExpressionNode and convert it with .into() (or pass it to Expression::new). Match on expression.node(), which borrows an &ExpressionNode. Cloning an Expression shares its immutable node instead of recursively copying its children. To change an expression, construct a new node. Common nodes also have Expression::literal, Expression::column, and Expression::function constructors.

For example, replace direct Expression::Literal(...) construction and matching with:

use spark_connect::expression::{Expression, ExpressionNode, LiteralExpression};

let expression: Expression = ExpressionNode::Literal(LiteralExpression::Long(1)).into();
let shared = expression.clone();
match shared.node() {
    ExpressionNode::Literal(LiteralExpression::Long(value)) => assert_eq!(*value, 1),
    _ => panic!("expected a long literal"),
}

Child expressions are handles too: ExpressionNode::DirectShufflePartitionId takes an Expression, and CaseWhen::else_expr is Option<Expression>, without the previous extra Box.

Logical-plan child fields now use Arc<LogicalPlan> instead of Box<LogicalPlan>. When constructing variants directly, replace Box::new(child) with Arc::new(child), or clone an existing Arc to share that child. Plan-building helpers accept impl Into<Arc<LogicalPlan>>, so they accept either an owned LogicalPlan or an existing Arc<LogicalPlan>. Serialization still produces the same protobuf tree; sharing does not deduplicate repeated relations on the wire.

LogicalPlan implements Drop, so that a plan of many levels is dropped without recursing. A field can therefore not be moved out of an owned LogicalPlan: destructuring one by value is a compile error (E0509). Match on a reference instead (match &plan, or match plan.as_ref() of an Arc<LogicalPlan>) and clone the fields you need; the inputs are Arcs, so cloning them shares them.

LogicalPlan::Raw adds a depth field: the levels of its relation as a plan, with those of the DataFrames that it holds, as pyspark.ml builds a relation over its input. They count for MAX_PLAN_DEPTH, as PySpark's serializer counts the plan of the input within its own. Code that constructs the variant directly sets it to 1 for a relation without nested plans. LogicalPlan::try_to_proto serializes a plan as a request does: a plan deeper than MAX_PLAN_DEPTH, or with an expression deeper than MAX_EXPRESSION_DEPTH, is a RecursionError. to_proto still serializes a plan of any depth, but prost encodes and drops a protobuf by recursing, so the proto of a plan of many thousands of levels can overflow a small stack.

Value and LiteralExpression add a YearMonthInterval(i32) variant for signed months. Collect gives it for a year-month interval, where it gave the text of the interval (Value::String("1-0")), so that a pivot on collected values names its columns as the pivot without values does (INTERVAL '1-0' YEAR TO MONTH), and create_dataframe takes it for an INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH column (not for INTERVAL YEAR or INTERVAL MONTH, which the server cannot narrow the Arrow interval to). Downstream exhaustive matches on these enums must handle the new variant. The Python client still raises NOT_IMPLEMENTED when it collects a year-month interval, as PySpark does.

DataFrame::repartition_by_range and repartition_by_range_opt return a Result. As PySpark's repartitionByRange, a partition count that is not positive is VALUE_NOT_POSITIVE and an empty column list CANNOT_BE_EMPTY. Before, the server split the rows round-robin for an empty column list. StatFunctions::sample_by returns a Result too: a stratum that is not a literal of a bool, an integer, a float or a string (a null, a decimal, binary, a date, a timestamp, an interval or an array) is DISALLOWED_TYPE_FOR_CONTAINER, as PySpark rejects a key that is not a float, an int or a str. Before, it was sent as an empty literal, which failed only when the DataFrame ran, or as its own literal, which sampled no rows. Without a seed, sample_by sends one that the client draws, as sample and random_split do.

A panic of a native StreamingQueryListener on an event of the listener bus is isolated, as on the started event and as PySpark isolates the exception of a listener: it is reported, the other listeners still get the event, and the subscription goes on. Before, it ended the subscription and removed every listener. An error that try_on_event returns still ends it.

The random functions rand, randn, uuid, shuffle, uniform, randstr and count_min_sketch draw a new seed for each call, as PySpark and the Scala client do. Before, each sent the same fixed seed, so two uuid() columns, or the uuid() of two runs, were equal. For reproducible values, use the _with_seed variants (rand_with_seed(42), uuid_with_seed(lit(42)), ...). random and random_with_seed are added as the aliases of rand that PySpark has.

DataFrameWriter::clear_bucket_by is added: it unsets the bucketing of a writer, so that its write sends none, as PySpark's bucketBy of a count that is not positive, the last bucketBy winning. bucket_by is unchanged and sends the count it is given.

DataFrame::persist takes impl Into<Option<StorageLevel>>, so a StorageLevel is passed as before. None sends no storage level, as PySpark's persist(None), and the server then caches at its spark.sql.defaultCacheStorageLevel. cache is unchanged and persists at MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER.

DataType::from_json reads the spatial types as the JSON reader of Spark does: a bare geometry or geography is of SRID 4326, geography(<algorithm>) is of the CRS OGC:CRS84, a CRS is of the form <authority>:<code>, and an algorithm other than SPHERICAL is ST_INVALID_ALGORITHM_VALUE. It no longer takes geometry(<srid>), geometry(any) and their geography forms, which are of the DDL, not of the JSON, of Spark. DataType::from_ddl takes a number or any as an SRID, as the DDL parser of Spark does, and no longer takes such forms as geometry(+5), geometry(SRID:ANY) or geography(4326, SPHERICAL).

docs.title: Native ML objects: fetch, summaries, save and load (Rust API)
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml reads and writes the server-side objects of Spark Connect ML as PySpark 4.3.0 does over Spark Connect, for the typed model accessors, summaries and persistence of the native classes to build on:

  • MlRef is a server-side object: a fitted model (Model::ml_ref), or another object that a fetch returns, such as a tree of an ensemble. Its clones and the DataFrames whose plans read it share it, and the last owner to drop deletes it on the server, as PySpark's RemoteModelRef.
  • fetch(&MlTarget, method, args) runs a method of an object, as _call_java of pyspark.ml does over Spark Connect (a Fetch command). MlTarget::object(&model_ref).child("summary") reaches the object of a method chain ("<id>.summary"), and MlTarget::helper(&session) the ML helper (invoke_helper_attr). Its result is a value (MlValue), new objects (an id list that names the trees of an ensemble is one object per tree), or a string. When the server has lost a summary with its offloaded model, the fetch recreates the summary of the target's summary dataset (CreateSummary) and runs once more, as PySpark does.
  • MlValue is a value as deserialize_param reads it and serialize_param sends it: ML vectors and matrices, scalars, strings and arrays, byte for byte as PySpark's literals (tests/golden/ml_values.json). An empty array, or one whose first element is null, has no type to infer: send it as FetchArg::Typed, as PySpark sends a (value, DataType) pair.
  • attribute_relation(&MlTarget, method, args) is the DataFrame of a method, as invoke_remote_attribute_relation reads it, of the summary dataset of a summary target. It keeps the object and the plans of its DataFrame arguments alive.
  • write_operator and write_object save an estimator, transformer or evaluator, or a fitted model (Write), and read loads one of its JVM class (Read), as RemoteMLWriter and RemoteMLReader of pyspark.ml.connect.readwrite. A loaded model is a new MlRef.
  • Model::write(), Estimator::write() and Evaluator::write() return an MlWriter, as PySpark's write() returns an MLWriter: .overwrite(), .option(key, value) and .save(path). A model saves of the session that holds it. An estimator or an evaluator, which holds no session, saves of the one that .session(&spark) sets (as MLWriter.session), since the Rust client has no active session.
  • The fit of the Estimator trait returns a Box<dyn Model>; model.downcast_ref::<M>() gives its concrete model type. Model::describe() is the server's description of a model (PySpark's __repr__ of a model, its toString). PredictionModel gives num_features() and predict(&vector), the members of every prediction model of pyspark.ml.

docs.title: Native LogisticRegression
docs.text:
The native spark_connect::ml::LogisticRegression fits Spark's JVM org.apache.spark.ml.classification.LogisticRegression through the Connect ML protocol. Its training features must be ML vectors, in the Rust API as in Python; convert an array column with array_to_vector before fitting. The Python class, pyspark.ml.connect.classification.LogisticRegression, follows pyspark.ml.classification.LogisticRegression, PySpark's standard API over Spark Connect, not the deprecated PyTorch class of pyspark.ml.connect. Its keyword-only constructor takes the 21 params of pyspark.ml's, with its defaults and TypeConverters: featuresCol, labelCol, predictionCol, maxIter, regParam, elasticNetParam, tol, fitIntercept, threshold, thresholds, probabilityCol, rawPredictionCol, standardization, weightCol, aggregationDepth, family, the matrices lowerBoundsOnCoefficients and upperBoundsOnCoefficients, the vectors lowerBoundsOnIntercepts and upperBoundsOnIntercepts, and maxBlockSizeInMB. It has a setter of each, and setParams. A fit sends a matrix or a vector as PySpark's ML serializer sends a DenseMatrix, a SparseMatrix or a vector; in the Rust API, Params::set_param_matrix sends an MlMatrix so. The params of the PyTorch training of the deprecated class (numTrainWorkers, batchSize, learningRate, momentum and seed) raise the TypeError of an unexpected keyword argument. As pyspark.ml's, the constructor and setParams raise PySpark's ValueError when the threshold and the thresholds that are set disagree (setParams leaves the params that it is given set), and setThreshold and setThresholds leave the other one set, as they do over Spark Connect, where the clear of pyspark.ml does nothing: a fit then sends both, and the JVM raises its error when they disagree. Its model outputs the columns of the JVM model, as pyspark.ml's does: a rawPrediction and a probability vector, and a double prediction. The JVM checks the labels (an integer in [0, 100), not null), the types of the columns, and the output columns that the DataFrame has already, and raises its errors, as with pyspark.ml: the client makes no checks of its own, and sends no query of the labels.

Fitting returns a server-cached model. Prediction uses that model's object reference and must use the same Spark session. Models are obtained through Estimator::fit; direct struct construction of LogisticRegressionModel is no longer supported. The cached model stays available while the model, a clone of it, or a DataFrame that it transformed is alive, including when such a DataFrame is executed later. When the last of them is dropped, the cached model is deleted on the server, as pyspark.ml does, without waiting for the server; a fit that is dropped at once leaves nothing cached.

The Rust transform of a fitted model rejects a DataFrame of another session. In Python, as with PySpark, it returns a DataFrame whose analysis or execution fails on the server of that session with CONNECT_ML.CACHE_INVALID.

The native estimators, transformers and evaluators of pyspark.ml.connect take keyword-only constructor parameters. The evaluators follow standard pyspark.ml.evaluation: multiclass classification defaults to metricName="f1", and binary classification uses rawPredictionCol="rawPrediction". Each value is converted by the TypeConverters of its param in PySpark (an integral float for an int param, for example), and a value that the converter rejects raises its TypeError. A fit, transform or evaluate sends only the params that the constructor or a setter set, so the server applies its defaults to the others, as with PySpark. An int beyond a long raises PySpark's VALUE_NOT_BETWEEN at the next fit. None is sent as a null literal, as PySpark sends it: the server reads a null bootstrap as false and rejects the other nulls. A param that is not given is not sent, so the server's default applies. A list param without elements is accepted by its constructor and setters, and a fit, transform or evaluate raises PySpark's CANNOT_INFER_ARRAY_ELEMENT_TYPE for it, as PySpark's serialization does.

A native class has the setParams of its pyspark.ml class. It is keyword-only, takes the params of the constructor, sets the params that it is given, in order, and returns the object, as PySpark's _set does. As PySpark's, the setParams of LogisticRegression then checks its threshold and thresholds, whichever call set them, as its constructor does. Its signature is PySpark's for every class, the feature stages included, except CrossValidator, which takes numFolds, parallelism and seed, with a default of None for the first two. The params argument of a fit, transform or evaluate, which pyspark.ml takes as a param map, is accepted: None and an empty dict leave the params as they are. The native classes have no Param objects to key a map by, so a non-empty map raises a TypeError that says the native classes take no param map. A list or tuple of maps to a fit is fitted as pyspark.ml fits it: one model per map, in order, returned as a list, so that [] fits nothing and does not read the dataset. Any other value raises the TypeError that pyspark.ml raises for it. The params argument is checked first, before the dataset, as pyspark.ml checks it.

Native fit, transform and evaluate require a Spark DataFrame, matching the dataset contract of standard pyspark.ml over Spark Connect. Passing a pandas DataFrame raises TypeError before the params of the class are validated, the schema is read or any request is sent (the helper calls below raise PySpark's error of its serialization); only a params argument that is not a param map is checked before it (see above). This also applies to empty pandas DataFrames and to the native Pipeline and CrossValidator placeholders. Convert local data explicitly with df = spark.createDataFrame(pdf) before calling estimator.fit(df), model.transform(df) or evaluator.evaluate(df). Transforms return Spark DataFrames; call toPandas() explicitly when a local result is needed. The deprecated pyspark.ml.connect pandas contract is not the target for these native methods. The feature stages described below use the same Spark DataFrame contract.

Another object than a DataFrame raises the AttributeError of sparkSession, the attribute that pyspark.ml reads of the dataset first ('int' object has no attribute 'sparkSession' of fit(5)), before any request; an object that has a sparkSession raises a TypeError. The methods that pyspark.ml runs as a helper or attribute call (PowerIterationClustering.assignClusters, PrefixSpan.findFrequentSequentialPatterns, and ALSModel.recommendForUserSubset and recommendForItemSubset) read nothing of their dataset. PySpark's serialization (pyspark.ml.connect.serialize) converts any other object to a literal, as LiteralExpression._from_value does: - One that cannot be a literal raises PySpark's error of the conversion. That includes a pandas DataFrame, which raises UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE here rather than the TypeError above, as with pyspark.ml, and an empty list, which raises CANNOT_INFER_ARRAY_ELEMENT_TYPE. - PySpark sends the others for the server to reject. These include an ML vector or matrix and a (value, DataType) pair, which it sends as they are. Here they raise a TypeError before any request.

As with pyspark.ml, a fit sends the DataFrame as it is, and the transform of a model is the transform of the DataFrame as it is, which sends no request: the JVM estimators and models check the columns, and raise their errors of a column of a wrong type, or of an output column that the DataFrame has already, in the fit, or when the transformed DataFrame is analyzed or run.

The column params of a fit and of a transform are sent as they are given, as pyspark.ml sends them, and the JVM reads a column by its exact name: featuresCol="Features" of a column features raises the JVM's FIELD_NOT_FOUND in a fit, as with pyspark.ml, while some JVM models resolve such a name. Evaluators send column names and types unchanged too, leaving their validation to Spark as standard pyspark.ml.evaluation does. Their metric results are Spark's double-precision values.

The native estimators take the VectorUDT features of pyspark.ml: the JVM raises its error of an array featuresCol (Column features must be of type class org.apache.spark.ml.linalg.VectorUDT:... but was actually class org.apache.spark.sql.types.ArrayType:array<double>.), in the fit and when the transformed DataFrame is analyzed. Convert an array column with pyspark.ml.functions.array_to_vector first, as for pyspark.ml. (The JVM KMeans, BisectingKMeans, GaussianMixture and LDA also take arrays whose elements cannot be null, which the arrays of createDataFrame can be.)

The feature stages, including StandardScaler and MaxAbsScaler, use Spark's JVM implementations through Connect. Vector-valued inputs must use VectorUDT; convert numeric arrays explicitly with pyspark.ml.functions.array_to_vector. StandardScaler defaults to withMean=False, withStd=True, matching standard pyspark.ml.

docs.title: Native RandomForestRegressor
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::RandomForestRegressor fits Spark's JVM random forest regressor through Connect using ML vector features and numeric labels. Rust builder setters and getters cover all 19 PySpark constructor parameters, including instance weights, bootstrap sampling, feature sampling and optional per-tree leaf indices. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults; a seed can select another reproducible sample.

The native Python estimator is available from pyspark.ml.connect.regression.RandomForestRegressor and pyspark.ml.connect.RandomForestRegressor. It uses PySpark's keyword-only constructor names, defaults and parameter conversions, with mutating setters. Fitted models expose DataFrame transform for the fitting session. Models, clones and lazy transformed DataFrames retain the cached server model until their last owner drops. Tree inspection, feature importances, single-vector prediction and persistence are not exposed by this native addition.

docs.title: Native GBTRegressor
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::GBTRegressor fits Spark's JVM gradient-boosted regressor through Connect with ML vector features and continuous numeric labels. Rust setters/getters cover all 22 PySpark constructor parameters. It supports squared and absolute loss, instance weights, row/feature sampling, learning rate, iteration limits and validation-set early stopping.

The Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.regression.GBTRegressor and pyspark.ml.connect.GBTRegressor. Its keyword-only signature and 21 named setters match PySpark. validationTol has no Python setter. The reference's signature advertises validationTol=0.1, but omitting it leaves the parameter unset and uses Spark's 0.01 default. This binding preserves that behavior; GBTRegressor(validationTol=0.1) explicitly sends 0.1. The Rust getter returns 0.01 when unset.

maxIter limits boosting iterations, and stepSize scales each tree after the first. With validationIndicatorCol, false rows train and true rows validate; early stopping can fit fewer trees. DataFrame transforms expose predictions and an optional vector of leaf IDs, one per fitted tree. Models, clones and lazy transformed DataFrames retain the cached model in its fitting session until the last owner is dropped. Tree inspection, per-iteration evaluation, single-vector prediction and persistence are outside this native addition.

docs.title: Native GBTClassifier
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::GBTClassifier fits Spark's JVM gradient-boosted binary classifier through Connect with ML vector features and labels 0 or 1. Rust builder setters/getters cover all 22 PySpark constructor parameters, plus probability/raw prediction column names and class thresholds. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults. A seed controls split-candidate row sampling, subsampling and feature sampling.

The Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.classification.GBTClassifier and pyspark.ml.connect.GBTClassifier. Its keyword-only constructor mirrors PySpark. Probability/raw prediction column names and thresholds are set through setProbabilityCol, setRawPredictionCol and setThresholds. validationTol is a constructor argument; PySpark does not provide a Python setter for it.

maxIter limits boosting iterations, and stepSize scales each tree after the first. With validationIndicatorCol, false rows train the trees and true rows validate early stopping; the resulting ensemble can contain fewer than maxIter trees. DataFrame transforms expose predictions, probabilities, raw margins and an optional vector of leaf IDs, one per fitted tree. Instance weights are supported. Models, clones and lazy transformed DataFrames retain the cached model in its fitting session until the last owner is dropped. Multiclass training, model inspection, per-iteration evaluation, single-vector prediction and persistence are outside this native addition.

docs.title: Native DecisionTreeRegressor
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::DecisionTreeRegressor fits Spark's JVM decision tree regressor through Connect with ML vector features and continuous numeric labels. Rust builder setters/getters cover all 16 PySpark constructor parameters, including set_variance_col, set_weight_col and set_leaf_col. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults.

The native Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.regression.DecisionTreeRegressor and pyspark.ml.connect.DecisionTreeRegressor. Its keyword-only constructor mirrors PySpark's parameter names and defaults. Mutating setFeaturesCol, setMaxDepth, setVarianceCol, etc. methods return the estimator.

Fitted models expose DataFrame transform, including predictions, optional weighted label variance in the predicted leaf and optional scalar double leaf indices. Variance is computed within the predicted leaf; it is not a confidence interval for the prediction. Models, clones and lazy transformed DataFrames keep the cached server model alive in its fitting session until the last owner is dropped. Tree inspection, feature importances, single-vector prediction and persistence are outside this addition.

docs.title: Native DecisionTreeClassifier
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::DecisionTreeClassifier trains Spark's JVM decision tree classifier through Connect with ML vector features and non-negative integer class labels below numClasses. Rust builder setters cover all 18 PySpark constructor parameters, including pruneTree (Spark 4.3.0), plus class thresholds. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults.

The Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.classification.DecisionTreeClassifier and pyspark.ml.connect.DecisionTreeClassifier. Its keyword-only constructor matches PySpark's parameter names and defaults; mutating setFeaturesCol, setMaxDepth, etc. methods and setThresholds return the estimator.

Fitted models expose DataFrame transform, including prediction, probability, raw per-leaf weighted class counts and an optional scalar double leaf index. Models, clones and lazy transformed DataFrames retain the cached model in its fitting session until the last owner is dropped. Tree inspection, feature importances, single-vector prediction and persistence are outside this addition.

docs.title: Native RandomForestClassifier
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::RandomForestClassifier trains Spark's JVM random forest classifier through Connect with ML vector features and non-negative integer class labels below numClasses. Rust builder setters cover all 22 PySpark constructor parameters, including pruneTree (Spark 4.3.0), plus class thresholds. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults. Without a seed, the sampling uses Spark's default seed (the hash of the class name), as with PySpark, so fits are reproducible either way.

The native Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.classification.RandomForestClassifier and pyspark.ml.connect.RandomForestClassifier. Its keyword-only constructor matches PySpark's parameter names and defaults, with mutating setFeaturesCol, setNumTrees, etc. methods and setThresholds.

Fitted models expose DataFrame transform, including prediction, probability, raw prediction and optional per-tree leaf index columns. Models, clones and lazy transformed DataFrames retain the cached model in its fitting session until the last owner is dropped. Tree inspection, feature importances, training summaries, single-vector prediction and persistence are not exposed by this native addition.

docs.title: Native KMeans
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::KMeans fits Spark's JVM K-means estimator with ML vector features through the Connect ML protocol. Rust builder setters cover all 12 constructor parameters, including set_k, set_seed, set_weight_col, set_distance_measure and set_solver. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults. Without a seed, the initialization uses Spark's default seed (the hash of the class name), as with PySpark, so fits are reproducible either way. Cluster numbers are arbitrary: compare membership rather than relying on particular numeric labels.

The native Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.clustering.KMeans and pyspark.ml.connect.KMeans, with the upstream keyword-only constructor and mutating parameter setters. Fitted models expose DataFrame transform in the fitting session. Models, clones and transformed DataFrames keep the cached server model alive until the last owner is dropped. Cluster-center access, training summaries, single-vector prediction and persistence are not exposed by this native addition. The vendored pyspark.ml.clustering API is unchanged.

docs.title: Native LinearRegression
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::LinearRegression fits Spark's JVM linear regression estimator through the Connect ML protocol, with ML vector features and numeric labels. Rust builder setters cover all 15 constructor parameters, including regularization, instance weights, solver selection and squared-error or Huber loss. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults.

The native Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.regression.LinearRegression and pyspark.ml.connect.LinearRegression. Its keyword-only constructor matches the JVM PySpark estimator's parameter names and defaults, with mutating setFeaturesCol, setRegParam, etc. methods. Fitted models expose transform on DataFrames from the fitting session. The model, its clones and transformed DataFrames keep the cached server model alive until the last owner is dropped. Model inspection (coefficients, intercept and summaries), single-vector prediction and persistence are not exposed by this native addition.

docs.title: Native LinearSVC
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::LinearSVC trains Spark's JVM binary linear support vector classifier through the Connect ML protocol. Use vector features and labels 0 or 1. Rust builder setters cover all 13 constructor parameters, including set_reg_param, set_tol, set_weight_col and set_threshold. Unset parameters use Spark's defaults. The Python binding is available as pyspark.ml.connect.classification.LinearSVC and pyspark.ml.connect.LinearSVC, with the upstream keyword-only constructor parameters and mutating setFeaturesCol, setRegParam, etc. methods.

fit returns a server-cached model; transform must use the fitting session. Clones and lazy prediction DataFrames keep the cached model usable while they are alive. When the last of the model, its clones and the DataFrames it transformed is dropped, the server deletes the cached model, as pyspark.ml does. The Python model uses the existing MLModel.transform interface. Model inspection (coefficients, intercept and summaries), single-vector prediction and model persistence are not exposed by this addition.

docs.title: Native Pipeline and CrossValidator: fit is not implemented
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::Pipeline and spark_connect::ml::CrossValidator, and their Python classes pyspark.ml.connect.Pipeline and pyspark.ml.connect.CrossValidator, do not fit. Their fit raises NOT_IMPLEMENTED (PySparkNotImplementedError in Python), naming Pipeline.fit or CrossValidator.fit, before any request is sent, and returns no model. The Connect ML protocol cannot run either one: the native Pipeline holds stage names, which the server cannot fit, and it has no pipeline model to transform; the native CrossValidator holds its numeric params only, without the estimator, evaluator or param grid. Their constructors and setters still set the params, as before.

To fit a pipeline or to tune a model from Python, use the vendored pyspark.ml.Pipeline and pyspark.ml.tuning.CrossValidator, which take the estimator and transformer objects, as PySpark does. The Rust API has no way to fit a pipeline or to tune a model.

docs.title: pyspark.ml
docs.text:
The DataFrame-based pyspark.ml API (pyspark.ml.classification, feature, regression, clustering, evaluation, tuning, stat, Pipeline, ...) is Apache Spark's own, vendored from v4.3.0: estimators fit, models transform, and pipelines save and load on the server as with PySpark Connect, over the Rust transport. These modules build their own spark.connect messages with the generated pyspark.sql.connect.proto, which needs the protobuf package (pip install "protobuf>=6.33.5"). The package is not a dependency of pyspark-client-rust: without it, pyspark.ml imports, but a fit or a transform raises an AttributeError that names protobuf.

A DataFrame of a plan of pyspark.ml (DataFrame(plan, session)) takes the plan ID of this client rather than the one of the plan, which its columns refer to.

docs.title: Spark Declarative Pipelines CLI
docs.text: The CLI of Spark Declarative Pipelines (python -m pyspark.pipelines.cli init, run and dry-run) and its modules are Apache Spark's own, vendored from v4.3.0, and Apache Spark's tests of them pass with this client. The CLI needs pyyaml and protobuf, which, as for pyspark.ml, are not dependencies of pyspark-client-rust. The user context extensions of a client (spark.client.add_threadlocal_user_context_extension and add_global_user_context_extension), which the CLI adds for the analyses of a pipeline, are sent with the requests of executions, analyses, configurations, error details and interrupts, as PySpark sends them.

docs.title: How parity is verified
docs.text:
Two independent gates in CI cover the two halves of a Spark Connect client - plan building and the transport/result path:

  • Golden-proto tests assert that the spark.connect protobuf plans this client builds (plans, expressions, and every SQL function) match the reference client byte-for-byte. This guards plan-building correctness.
  • The official Apache Spark Connect test suite runs the standard PySpark tests against this client, exercising the transport and Arrow result paths end-to-end against a real server. See the official-test-suite notes and the CI notes under dev/design/.

Together the two gates cover what the client sends and what it does with what comes back.

docs.title: The parity ledger
docs.text:
Coverage is tracked mechanically. scripts/gen_parity_ledger.py AST-parses the reference PySpark source and emits one row per public class, function, and method into a ledger (dev/parity/inventory.csv), so nothing is silently dropped. The current inventory covers roughly:

Kind Count Methods ~1340 Functions ~620 Classes ~300

Each row carries a status:

  • done / verified - mirrored by the client (and, where applicable, confirmed against the reference).
  • n/a - architecture-satisfied: the equivalent wire behavior is provided by the Rust core (spark-connect / -core / -proto), so a reference-private or generated symbol is not mirrored one-to-one.

The ledger is a development tracking tool (kept under dev/parity/); the official test suite is the authoritative gate.

docs.title: What "drop-in" means
docs.text:
From Python, pyspark-client-rust replaces the pyspark-client package: same import pyspark, same public API, same server - see Installation. Use it exactly like PySpark. The native Rust API mirrors the same surface.

The drop-in parses the protobufs that a pickled Column or DataFrame carries, and the requests that session hooks see, at any depth that PySpark's serializer reaches, where the parsers of protobuf and prost stop at 100 nested messages. Its Rust client enables prost's no-recursion-limit feature, which applies to every message the drop-in decodes. So it also decodes server responses deeper than 100 nested messages, such as the schema of a struct nested 34 levels deep, which PySpark's client rejects with "Exception deserializing response!". The server is trusted, as SECURITY.md sets out, so this is not a bound on the responses.

An Observation that PySpark pickled at protocol 0 or 1 raises a TypeError when the drop-in unpickles it, as CPython's copyreg._reconstructor cannot create the drop-in's Observation, a class with a native base; protocols 2 and up, pickle's default, load in both clients, and PySpark loads the drop-in's at every protocol.

The TypeError for too many positional arguments counts them without self: where CPython says "takes from 2 to 4 positional arguments but 5 were given", the drop-in says "takes from 1 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given". A method that takes no arguments gets "takes no arguments (1 given)", where CPython says "takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given" for DataFrame.distinct(1). A method that takes one argument gets the plural "positional arguments" even for a count of one: the drop-in says "takes 1 positional arguments but 3 were given" for DataFrame.limit(1, 2, 3), where CPython says "takes 2 positional arguments but 4 were given". A warning that the Rust core raises, such as the FutureWarning of registerTempTable, is attributed to the caller's frame and module, so a warnings.filterwarnings(..., module="pyspark") does not match it, as it matches PySpark's.

The TypeError for a bad keyword argument of a method that takes no **options is PyO3's, which CPython words differently in two cases. For a key that is not a str, as df.limit(1, **{1: 2}), CPython says "keywords must be strings", where the drop-in says "DataFrame.limit() got an unexpected keyword argument '1'". For a method that takes no arguments, as df.count(foo=1), CPython says "DataFrame.count() got an unexpected keyword argument 'foo'", where the drop-in says "DataFrame.count() takes no keyword arguments". The methods that take **options, and the readers', writers' and SparkSession.builder.config's that take named options, word both as CPython does.

docs.title: Native NaiveBayes
docs.text:
The Rust ml::NaiveBayes and ml::NaiveBayesModel train and predict through Spark Connect's cached-model protocol. The Rust-backed Python API exports NaiveBayes from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.classification; fit returns the shared native MLModel, whose transform produces DataFrame predictions.

All nine PySpark constructor parameters and named setters are supported: featuresCol, labelCol, predictionCol, probabilityCol, rawPredictionCol, smoothing, modelType, thresholds and weightCol. Rust exposes corresponding builder setters and getters. Unset parameters are omitted so the server uses its defaults. The Python constructor is keyword-only and converts values with PySpark's parameter converters.

All four model types are covered by live tests: multinomial, bernoulli, complement and gaussian. Multinomial/complement inputs must be nonnegative; Bernoulli inputs must be binary; Gaussian inputs may contain continuous negative values. Tests also cover multiclass dense/sparse inputs, probability/raw score columns, smoothing and instance weights, threshold decisions, suppressed vector outputs, independent fits, session isolation and lazy model lifetime. A golden fixture captures all nine parameters for each model type from official PySpark.

This native surface covers construction, parameter setters, fit and DataFrame transform. Model coefficient/statistic inspection, single-vector prediction and persistence are outside this surface. The vendored pyspark.ml.classification API continues to use its existing implementation.

docs.title: Native BisectingKMeans
docs.text:
The Rust ml::BisectingKMeans and ml::BisectingKMeansModel support training and DataFrame cluster assignment through Spark Connect's cached-model protocol. Python exports the native estimator from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.clustering; fit returns the shared native MLModel.

All eight constructor parameters and named setters are supported: featuresCol, predictionCol, maxIter, seed, k, minDivisibleClusterSize, distanceMeasure and weightCol. Rust also provides parameter getters. The keyword-only Python constructor matches official PySpark's order/defaults and parameter conversions. Unset parameters are omitted so the server uses its defaults, including k=4.

Live tests cover hierarchical splitting, absolute/fractional minimum divisible cluster sizes (which may produce fewer than k leaves), instance weights, Euclidean/cosine distance, sparse/dense inputs, seeded reproducibility, independent fits, session isolation and lazy model lifetime. Golden fixtures compare all eight parameters at six signed seed/integer-width boundaries with official PySpark.

This native API covers construction, setters, fit and DataFrame transform. Cluster-center/summary/cost inspection, single-vector prediction and persistence are outside this surface. The vendored pyspark.ml.clustering API retains its existing implementation.

docs.title: Native GeneralizedLinearRegression
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::GeneralizedLinearRegression fits Spark's JVM estimator and returns a cached GeneralizedLinearRegressionModel. Python exposes it from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.regression; fit returns the shared native MLModel.

All 16 PySpark constructor parameters and named setters are available: labelCol, featuresCol, predictionCol, family, link, fitIntercept, maxIter, tol, regParam, weightCol, solver, linkPredictionCol, variancePower, linkPower, offsetCol and aggregationDepth. Rust provides builder setters and getters for each parameter. Unset optional parameters stay unset: Spark chooses the family default link, or the Tweedie link power from variancePower.

Fitting accepts ML vector features and numeric labels. Transform produces predictions and, when requested, the linear predictor in linkPredictionCol. Instance weights, offsets and L2 regularization are handled by Spark. The same numerical tests run against official PySpark and the native Python client, covering all five families (Gaussian, binomial, Poisson, Gamma and Tweedie), default and explicit links, dense/sparse features, weights, offsets, independent fitted models, lazy model ownership and rejected inputs. Official PySpark golden fixtures verify the parameter encoding, and live Rust tests exercise fitting and prediction directly.

This native API covers construction, setters, fitting and DataFrame transforms. Coefficient/intercept access, model summaries, evaluation, persistence and single-vector prediction are not exposed by this addition.

docs.title: Native GaussianMixture
docs.text:
Rust ml::GaussianMixture and ml::GaussianMixtureModel train Gaussian mixture models and produce cluster assignments and component probabilities through Spark Connect's cached-model protocol. Python exports the native estimator from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.clustering; fit returns the shared native MLModel.

All nine constructor parameters and named setters are supported: featuresCol, predictionCol, k, probabilityCol, tol, maxIter, seed, aggregationDepth and weightCol. Rust also provides corresponding getters. The keyword-only Python constructor matches official PySpark's order/defaults and conversions. Unset values are omitted so the server uses its defaults.

Live tests cover one- and two-dimensional mixtures, two/three components, normalized probabilities and assignments, dense/sparse vectors, weights, seeded reproducibility, independent fits, disabled probability output, server validation, session isolation and lazy model lifetime. Golden fixtures compare all nine parameters at six signed seed/integer-width boundaries with official PySpark.

The native surface covers construction, parameter setters, fit and DataFrame transform. Component/weight/covariance inspection, training summaries, single-vector prediction and persistence are outside this surface. The vendored pyspark.ml.clustering API retains its existing implementation.

docs.title: Native FMClassifier
docs.text: spark_connect::ml::FMClassifier and pyspark.ml.connect.classification.FMClassifier fit Spark's binary factorization machine classifier. All 17 PySpark constructor parameters have Rust builder setters/getters and named Python setters. Fitted models produce prediction, probability and raw-prediction columns, with configurable thresholds. Both the gd and adamW solvers run on the Spark server.

docs.title: Native MultilayerPerceptronClassifier
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::MultilayerPerceptronClassifier and its native Python binding support all 13 PySpark constructor parameters plus setThresholds. Configure layers before fitting; input and output sizes must match the feature dimension and number of classes. initialWeights accepts dense or sparse ML vectors: Rust uses MlVector (a Vec<f64> or array also converts to a dense vector), and Python accepts the values supported by PySpark's TypeConverters.toVector. Layer arrays and vector parameters are encoded in Rust and checked against fixtures captured with official PySpark.

The fitted model produces multiclass prediction, probability and raw-prediction columns. Both l-bfgs and gd are supported. As in PySpark, fitting an empty DataFrame can return a model; the native client preserves that server behavior.

docs.title: Native OneVsRest
docs.text:
spark_connect::ml::OneVsRest and pyspark.ml.connect.classification.OneVsRest implement the multiclass reduction in Rust. Supply a native binary classifier, for example OneVsRest::new().set_classifier(LinearSVC::new()) in Rust or OneVsRest(classifier=LinearSVC()) in Python. The Classifier enum accepts all eight native binary classifiers: LogisticRegression, LinearSVC, DecisionTreeClassifier, RandomForestClassifier, GBTClassifier, NaiveBayes, FMClassifier and MultilayerPerceptronClassifier. Perceptron base classifiers need a two-unit output layer.

All seven PySpark constructor parameters have named setters. Rust exposes scalar parameter getters and the configured classifier. Fits clone the base classifier for each class and run at most parallelism fits at once. Python observes mutations to the supplied classifier made before fit, while fitting leaves that classifier unchanged. Class indices run from zero through the maximum label, as in PySpark. Instance weights are forwarded when the base classifier supports them; Python warns when they are ignored for FMClassifier or the perceptron.

The model aggregates positive-class raw scores into rawPrediction and chooses the first highest score for prediction, ignoring NaN/null scores as PySpark does. It produces no probability column. Temporary columns and fit-created caches are cleaned up, and transformed DataFrames retain the binary models for lazy evaluation. Models must transform data in their fitting session.

These additions cover native estimator construction, parameters, fitting and DataFrame transforms. Model coefficient/weight inspection, training summaries, persistence and single-vector prediction remain separate API work.

docs.title: Native AFTSurvivalRegression, IsotonicRegression and FMRegressor
docs.text:
All eight regression estimators in PySpark 4.3.0 now have native Rust fit/transform implementations. The three additions are available under spark_connect::ml and pyspark.ml.connect.regression, and are re-exported from pyspark.ml.connect. They fit Spark's JVM estimators and retain the returned server-cached models for as long as a model clone or transformed DataFrame needs them.

  • AFTSurvivalRegression fits a Weibull accelerated failure time model. It accepts positive survival times and a censor column (1 for observed events, 0 for censored observations), and can produce a vector of requested quantiles. All 11 constructor parameters have Rust and Python setters, including quantileProbabilities, quantilesCol, and the aggregation/block-size settings.
  • IsotonicRegression fits increasing or decreasing univariate regression. It supports scalar features or a selected vector component (featureIndex), instance weights, interpolation between fitted boundaries, and clamping beyond the training range. All six constructor parameters have setters.
  • FMRegressor fits factorization machines with pairwise interactions and optional intercept and linear terms, using either adamW or gd. All 14 constructor parameters have setters, including factor size, initialization, mini-batch fraction, regularization and seed.

Unset parameters use Spark's defaults. The Python wrappers preserve PySpark's keyword-only constructor signatures and type conversion, and take ML vector features, as pyspark.ml's do.

This support covers construction, configuration, fitting and DataFrame transforms. Python returns the common MLModel. Specialized model inspection (e.g. AFT coefficients/scale, isotonic boundaries/predictions, FM factors), single-instance prediction and model persistence are not exposed by these native wrappers.

Parameter goldens come from official PySpark 4.3.0. Native Rust and Python tests exercise censoring and quantiles, weighted isotonic interpolation, both FM solvers, validation errors and cached-model lifetimes. The Python behavior tests also run unchanged against the official client.

docs.title: Native LDA and PowerIterationClustering
docs.text:
The native Rust and Python APIs now implement all five clustering algorithms in PySpark 4.3.0: KMeans, BisectingKMeans, GaussianMixture, LDA and PowerIterationClustering. This describes algorithm execution, not complete model-inspection or persistence parity.

Rust ml::LDA supports online and EM training and cached-model DataFrame transforms. Python exposes LDA through pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.clustering; fit returns the shared native MLModel. All 14 constructor parameters have Python setters and Rust builder setters/getters, including document/topic concentrations, learning settings, checkpoint settings, seed and topic-distribution output column. Both optimizers return a vector of topic probabilities per document; empty documents produce zero vectors. As with pyspark.ml, an array feature column is sent as it is, and the JVM rejects one whose elements may be null, such as the arrays of createDataFrame.

ml::PowerIterationClustering::assign_clusters and Python assignClusters build Spark Connect's powerIterationClusteringAssignClusters helper relation. This algorithm has no fit/transform API or fitted model. It accepts source/destination vertex columns and optional nonnegative edge weights, with k, maxIter and initMode settings, and returns a Spark DataFrame with id: bigint and cluster: int. Parameter values are captured when the relation is built. Omitting weightCol uses unweighted edges; an explicit null remains distinct from an omitted parameter and is validated by Spark. The lazy relation retains any cached models used by its input DataFrame.

Both APIs require Spark DataFrames and reject pandas inputs. Reference-derived golden fixtures and live tests cover both LDA optimizers, dense/sparse inputs, graph initialization modes, weighted/unweighted graphs, custom columns, setters, validation and model lifetime. LDA topic matrices, likelihood/perplexity methods, topic descriptions, distributed-model inspection/conversion and persistence are outside this native surface. The vendored pyspark.ml.clustering API retains its existing implementation.

docs.title: Native feature stages
docs.text:
All 38 standard pyspark.ml.feature estimators and transformers have native Rust execution and Python bindings. Rust exposes them as spark_connect::ml::<Name>, with typed builder setters/getters. Python exports them from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.feature, with standard pyspark.ml.feature keyword-only constructor signatures and named mutating setters. The vendored pyspark.ml.feature module is unchanged.

Area Stages Text and categorical features CountVectorizer, HashingTF, IDF, Word2Vec, Tokenizer, RegexTokenizer, NGram, StopWordsRemover, StringIndexer, IndexToString, OneHotEncoder, TargetEncoder, FeatureHasher Scaling and numeric transforms StandardScaler, MaxAbsScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler, Normalizer, Binarizer, Bucketizer, QuantileDiscretizer, Imputer, DCT, PolynomialExpansion, ElementwiseProduct Assembly and selection VectorAssembler, VectorIndexer, VectorSizeHint, VectorSlicer, Interaction, PCA, ChiSqSelector, UnivariateFeatureSelector, VarianceThresholdSelector, RFormula, SQLTransformer Locality-sensitive hashing BucketedRandomProjectionLSH, MinHashLSH

The 20 estimators fit through Spark Connect's ML command and return session-scoped cached models; Python returns the shared native MLModel. The 18 transformers build lazy ML relations. Transformed DataFrames retain their fitted models and upstream input plans. QuantileDiscretizer returns a cached JVM Bucketizer; its Rust model wrapper is named QuantileDiscretizerModel. Training-only parameters are omitted from model transforms. Multi-column parameters, nested Bucketizer splits, vector-valued ElementwiseProduct weights, NaN imputation values, and UnivariateFeatureSelector's setter-only parameters are supported.

StandardScaler and MaxAbsScaler exports now refer to the native implementations. This changes the previous deprecated pyspark.ml.connect scaler behavior: pandas frames and array-valued feature columns are rejected; transforms return Spark DataFrames containing vectors. Mean centering is opt-in through withMean=True. Convert pandas data with spark.createDataFrame and array columns with array_to_vector before fitting.

This covers constructor parameters, named setters, fit and DataFrame transform, and StopWordsRemover.loadDefaultStopWords, which reads the server's default stop words through Spark Connect's ML helper, as PySpark does (Rust StopWordsRemover::load_default_stop_words).

In Rust, each fitted model also has the members of its PySpark model class, which it reads of the server-side model as PySpark does: for example CountVectorizerModel::vocabulary, PCAModel::pc, the scaler statistics, VectorIndexerModel::category_maps, the LSH models' approx_nearest_neighbors and approx_similarity_join, and Word2VecModel::get_vectors and find_synonyms. CountVectorizerModel::from_vocabulary and StringIndexerModel::from_labels and from_arrays_of_labels build a model of given values, and QuantileDiscretizer::fit_bucketizer gives the Bucketizer of the fitted splits, as PySpark's fit does. Every stage and model saves with write() and loads with load(session, path), as PySpark's save and load. The Python classes gain these members with the native model classes. Pipeline/tuning execution is separate from this native surface. Existing vendored helper classes remain available.

Tests compare all 38 stages with official PySpark 4.3.0 parameter literals and Spark results, including 10 multi-column/parameter variants, both constructor and setter configuration, model lifetime, invalid inputs and pandas rejection. Schema checks compare class identifiers, nullability and ML metadata; Connect omits the backing SQL schema of JVM UDTs on the wire. Run scripts/capture_ml_features_golden.py with the official client to regenerate the fixture. scripts/capture_feature_models_golden.py captures the members of every fitted model, the class methods, and the save and load of every stage, which e2e_feature_models.rs compares. Native live tests run in CI; set FEATURE_REFERENCE=1 explicitly to run their reference mode.

docs.title: Native FPGrowth and PrefixSpan
docs.text:
Rust ml::FPGrowth fits Spark's frequent-itemset model and returns a typed FPGrowthModel. The model exposes lazy freq_itemsets() and association_rules() DataFrames and transform() predictions. The Python classes are exported from pyspark.ml.connect and pyspark.ml.connect.fpm; fitted models expose freqItemsets and associationRules as properties. All five estimator constructor parameters have named setters; model setters cover the item column, prediction column and minimum confidence. Parameters for prediction are captured when its lazy plan is built. The itemset/rule properties fetch the fitted server model, matching standard PySpark's Connect attribute relations.

Rust ml::PrefixSpan::find_frequent_sequential_patterns and Python PrefixSpan.findFrequentSequentialPatterns mine arrays of itemsets directly through the Connect helper, with all four constructor parameters and named setters. They return sequence/frequency DataFrames and have no fit/transform model.

These APIs accept Spark DataFrames and reject pandas frames before requests. Lazy model tables retain their cached model; PrefixSpan retains its input plan, including any upstream fitted models. Fitted-model transforms require the fitting session. Persistence is outside this native addition. The vendored pyspark.ml.fpm module is unchanged.

Spark 4.3.0's Connect helper currently rejects Long argument literals: PrefixSpan's maxLocalProjDBSize works within the signed 32-bit range, including its default 32,000,000; larger values raise the same LONG not supported server error as official PySpark. The client preserves PySpark's integer widths and explicit null parameters. Tests cover this limitation, typed string/integer itemsets, association rules, held-out predictions, model setters, sequence-length limits, invalid data, and model lifetime.

docs.title: Native ALS recommendation
docs.text:
ml::ALS / ml::ALSModel in Rust and pyspark.ml.connect.recommendation.ALS / ALSModel in the Rust-backed Python package run Spark's standard ALS over Connect. The estimator exposes all 18 parameters, including explicit/implicit feedback, nonnegative factors, regularization, block counts, storage levels and seed. Python mirrors the 17 official constructor keywords; use setPredictionCol for an alternate prediction column, and setNumBlocks to set both block counts.

The fitted model supports transform, rank, user/item factor tables, recommendations for all users/items, and recommendations for a subset of users/items. Rust uses user_factors, item_factors, and recommend_for_*; Python exposes userFactors, itemFactors, and recommendFor*. Model setters control transform parameters, including coldStartStrategy="drop" to remove predictions for unknown IDs. Factor and recommendation relations access the fitted server model, matching PySpark Connect. Lazy results retain their cached model and any models referenced by the subset DataFrame until evaluation completes.

Fit, transform and subset recommendation inputs must be Spark DataFrames; pandas DataFrames are rejected before conversion or RPC. Model operations must use the fit session. Official PySpark 4.3.0 fixtures cover explicit and implicit ratings, predictions, cold starts, factors, and all four recommendation methods, with live Rust and native Python tests. Model persistence is separate from these APIs.

docs.title: Native ML evaluators
docs.text:
Rust and the Rust-backed pyspark.ml.connect.evaluation exports provide all six standard Spark ML evaluators: regression, binary classification, multiclass classification, multilabel classification, clustering and ranking. Their constructor parameters and named setters follow pyspark.ml.evaluation in PySpark 4.3.0. Rust also provides typed parameter getters. Metric direction is available as is_larger_better() / isLargerBetter() without contacting Spark.

The three existing Python evaluator wrappers now use standard Spark ML defaults: BinaryClassificationEvaluator takes rawPredictionCol="rawPrediction", and MulticlassClassificationEvaluator defaults to metricName="f1" and requires keyword arguments. Use rawPredictionCol / setRawPredictionCol instead of the deprecated probabilityCol / setProbabilityCol binary-evaluator argument.
