Evaluation sends Spark DataFrames and their column names/types directly to Spark. Pandas DataFrames are rejected before serialization or RPC. Prepare double prediction columns, vector scores, and arrays of doubles where required by the corresponding standard evaluator. Clustering features may be vectors or arrays of doubles. Evaluators no longer silently cast columns, convert array scores to vectors, or normalize field-name casing.

Official PySpark fixtures and live Rust/Python tests cover every supported metric, weights, regression through the origin, binary score bins, multiclass log-loss clipping and beta, per-label metrics, both silhouette distances, ranking cutoffs, invalid inputs, and metric direction. Generic parameter-map APIs and evaluator persistence remain separate work.

docs.title: Native ML statistics
docs.text:
Rust's ml::{ChiSquareTest, Correlation, KolmogorovSmirnovTest, Summarizer, SummaryBuilder, MultivariateGaussian} and the native Python classes in pyspark.ml.stat cover the standard ML statistics APIs from PySpark 4.3.0. The Python module is a Rust-backed shim, replacing its vendored implementation, except MultivariateGaussian, which stays PySpark's plain Python class. The deprecated pyspark.ml.connect public API is excluded from statistics parity work; statistics have no new export under that namespace.

The statistical tests return lazy Spark DataFrames. Chi-square supports both the vector result and one row per feature (flatten=True); correlation supports Pearson and Spearman; the KS test supports Spark's normal distribution, with optional mean and standard deviation. Spark validates column types and statistical arguments. As with pyspark.ml.stat, the dataset and the other arguments are serialized as the arguments of a helper call, in that order, before any RPC (see the native ML helper calls above): a pandas DataFrame raises PySpark's UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE, an argument that cannot be a literal raises the error of its conversion, and a literal of another type than PySpark sends for the server to reject raises a TypeError. The KS test converts its parameters with float() first, as PySpark does. Results retain any fitted models used by their input plans.

Summarizer.metrics(...).summary(features, weight) builds a SQL aggregate that works in select and grouped aggregations. All ten metrics are supported: mean, sum, variance, std, count, numNonZeros, max, min, normL1, and normL2. Each also has a static convenience method; Rust uses snake_case (num_non_zeros, norm_l1, norm_l2). Omitted weights default to 1.0. Inputs are ML vector Columns, including sparse vectors. Metric names are case sensitive; numNonZeros uses a capital Z. An empty metric selection returns an empty struct.

MultivariateGaussian is a mutable mean/covariance holder, with no computation or extra validation. Rust uses MlVector and MlMatrix (dense or sparse storage, the matrix type of the native ML params). Python keeps PySpark's plain class, whose instances hold the original vector and matrix objects and pickle as PySpark's. Python results materialize vectors and matrices through the existing ML UDT conversion.

Reference protobuf fixtures and live Rust/Python tests cover every metric with and without weights, grouped summaries, chi-square flattening, both correlation methods, KS parameters, constant-feature NaNs, invalid inputs, and lazy model ownership. Python tests additionally compare sparse and dense inputs. Native classes are asserted explicitly; the tests also run separately with official PySpark as the reference.

docs.title: Configuration and Connection
docs.text: Configure connections to local or remote Spark Connect servers, set session parameters, and manage authentication.

docs.title: Connection String Format
docs.text:
Connection strings follow the format sc://host:port/;param=value. Parameters are optional:

Parameter Purpose Example token Authentication token, sent over TLS to any host but localhost sc://host:15002/;token=abc123 user_id User identity sc://host:15002/;user_id=alice session_id Session identifier sc://host:15002/;session_id=sess_xyz use_ssl Enable TLS sc://host:15002/;use_ssl=true

Note

TLS and authentication parameters are passed in the connection string. Consult your infrastructure team for any required credentials or certificates.

docs.title: Building a Session
docs.text:
use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .get_or_create()?;

// Session configuration is applied at runtime via `spark.conf()`:
spark.conf().set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "20")?;

docs.title: Runtime Configuration
docs.text:
Access and modify session configuration at runtime:

// Get a config value
let partitions = spark.conf().get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions")?;

// Set a config value
spark.conf().set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")?;

docs.title: Starting a Local Spark Connect Server
docs.text:
To run a Spark Connect server locally for development:

# Set SPARK_HOME to your Spark installation
export SPARK_HOME=/path/to/spark

# Start the server on sc://localhost:15002
$SPARK_HOME/sbin/start-connect-server.sh

The Spark distribution bundles the Spark Connect server, so it needs no --packages.

The server listens on port 15002 by default. To use a different port, add --conf spark.connect.grpc.binding.port=<port>.

Tip

The Spark Connect server requires a JVM and Apache Spark 4.3.0 or later. Stop it with $SPARK_HOME/sbin/stop-connect-server.sh.

docs.title: Remote Connections
docs.text:
To connect to a remote Spark Connect server:

use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
    .remote("sc://spark.example.com:15002/;token=YOUR_TOKEN")
    .get_or_create()?;

Replace spark.example.com, the port, and authentication parameters as needed. As in PySpark, a token implies TLS, so this connects over TLS. A token of the SPARK_CONNECT_AUTHENTICATE_TOKEN environment variable does the same. Only to localhost is a token sent without TLS, for local development; to 127.0.0.1 and [::1] it is sent over TLS, as in PySpark. Without a token, use_ssl=true turns TLS on:

use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
    .remote("sc://spark.example.com:15002/;use_ssl=true")
    .get_or_create()?;

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome. This is an Apache Software Foundation project, so a few conventions apply.

The repository holds the Rust client crates under crates/ and the Python drop-in: the pyspark package under python/pyspark, around the pyspark._pyspark extension that the crates/pyspark-rs crate builds. Architecture shows how they fit together.

docs.title: Issues and discussion
docs.text: Bugs and feature requests are tracked in ASF JIRA under the SPARK project - GitHub Issues are disabled. Reference the JIRA key in your pull request title, e.g. [SPARK-XXXXX][CONNECT] Short summary, with [PYTHON] after [CONNECT] for a change to the Python drop-in.

docs.title: Building and testing
docs.text:
Requires a Rust toolchain and protobuf-compiler. Non-Windows aarch64 builds also need the target C tools described in the source build requirements.

cargo build                 # build the library crates
cargo test                  # unit + golden-proto tests
cargo build -p examples     # the Rust-native examples

Builder correctness is covered by golden-proto tests: plans, expressions, and all SQL functions are asserted byte-for-byte against captured reference protos. Transport and Arrow paths are exercised by the end-to-end tests below and by the official Apache Spark Connect test suite in CI - see the CI notes under dev/design/.

The end-to-end tests (crates/spark-connect/tests/e2e_*.rs and a few others) run only when SPARK_REMOTE names a Spark Connect server; without it they pass without checking anything. They share one server session, so CI runs them on one thread:

SPARK_REMOTE=sc://localhost:15002 \
  cargo test -p apache-spark-connect --test e2e_dataframe -- --test-threads=1

The wasm-udf example crates need the wasm32 target and are built by manifest path (they're excluded from the workspace):

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo build --manifest-path examples/wasm-udf-inline/Cargo.toml

docs.title: A local Spark Connect server
docs.text:
The end-to-end tests, the live Python tests and the official test suites run against a Spark 4.3.0 Connect server. The Spark distribution bundles the server, so no --packages is needed: unpack spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3-connect.tgz (the one CI uses) or spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3.tgz from the Apache archive, and start it with Java 17 and CI's settings:

export SPARK_HOME=/path/to/spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3-connect
(cd "$SPARK_HOME" && TZ=UTC SPARK_TESTING=1 PYSPARK_PYTHON="$(command -v python)" \
  ./sbin/start-connect-server.sh \
  --driver-memory 3g --conf spark.sql.session.localRelationSizeLimit=1073741824)

It listens on sc://localhost:15002 and logs to $SPARK_HOME/logs; stop it with "$SPARK_HOME"/sbin/stop-connect-server.sh. The settings:

  • TZ=UTC makes UTC the session time zone, as on CI's runners. The test commands below set it too.
  • SPARK_TESTING=1 turns on Spark's test-mode defaults, which some tests rely on.
  • PYSPARK_PYTHON is the Python that runs UDFs on the server. It needs pandas and pyarrow, and the same minor version as the Python that runs the tests, or their UDFs fail with PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH. Start the server with the virtual environment active.
  • Starting it from $SPARK_HOME lets the official tests' relative data paths resolve.

docs.title: Python drop-in
docs.text: python/pyspark holds Rust-backed shims over pyspark._pyspark and code vendored from PySpark (see below). Its tests assert the behavior of official PySpark 4.3.0: where the two differ, PySpark is the reference (see Compatibility).

docs.title: Set up Python
docs.text:
The package supports Python 3.9 or later (requires-python in pyproject.toml); CI runs Python 3.11. Create a virtual environment with the packages CI installs. pandas stays below 3.0, which PySpark 4.3 does not fully support yet:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install pytest coverage 'pandas>=2.2,<3.0' pyarrow numpy grpcio grpcio-status \
  googleapis-common-protos cloudpickle zstandard py4j ruff==0.14.0

Tests that need an optional package skip without it; for the official suites, CI also installs 'plotly<6.0.0' and graphviz==0.20.3.

docs.title: Build the extension
docs.text:
Build the extension with the Rust requirements above, and copy it into the package. Repeat this after every change to the Rust code, including the Python sources that the extension embeds (crates/pyspark-rs/src/row.py and values.py):

cargo build -p pyspark-rs --release
cp target/release/lib_pyspark.dylib python/pyspark/_pyspark.so   # macOS
cp target/release/lib_pyspark.so python/pyspark/_pyspark.so      # Linux

python/ is then a working pyspark package. CI puts it on PYTHONPATH rather than installing it, which keeps it apart from any other pyspark in the environment:

PYTHONPATH=$(pwd)/python python -c "import pyspark; print(pyspark.__file__)"

To build a wheel instead, run maturin build --release --out dist, which reads [tool.maturin] in pyproject.toml (see Installation).

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
Run the tests from python/. The offline suites need no server:

cd python
TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m pytest \
  tests/test_dropin_offline.py tests/test_arrow_handoff.py tests/test_ml_offline.py
TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m pytest tests/test_dropin_offline.py -k pickle   # a subset

The live suites, tests/test_*_e2e.py, run against the local server and skip without SPARK_REMOTE:

SPARK_REMOTE=sc://localhost:15002 TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m pytest tests/test_*_e2e.py

CI runs the test files that its workflows name (coverage.yml for the offline suites, build_python_connect.yml for the live ones), so add a new test to an existing file, or add a new file to the workflow. CI also measures the coverage of the hand-written shim within the scope of python/.coveragerc, and fails below the floor that coverage.yml sets:

TZ=UTC PYTHONPATH=$(pwd) python -m coverage run --rcfile=.coveragerc -m pytest \
  tests/test_dropin_offline.py tests/test_arrow_handoff.py tests/test_ml_offline.py
python -m coverage report --rcfile=.coveragerc

docs.title: Run the official PySpark tests
docs.text:
On every pull request, CI runs Apache Spark's own Connect test suites twice: against the drop-in's classes, and with official PySpark sending its requests through the Rust transport. Run the files that cover your change with scripts/run_official_tests.py, from the repository root. --spark is an Apache Spark tree with the tests under python/: CI clones the v4.3.0 tag, and the unpacked distribution has the same test files.

RUST_PYSPARK_SO=$(pwd)/python/pyspark/_pyspark.so TZ=UTC python scripts/run_official_tests.py \
  --dropin --spark "$SPARK_HOME" --remote sc://localhost:15002 \
  --only pyspark/sql/tests/connect/test_parity_column.py

Without --dropin, the file runs through the transport instead. Without --only, the whole suite runs, which takes about an hour on CI (build_python_connect.yml has CI's exact options). The known failures are listed in scripts/dropin_known_failures.txt and scripts/parity_known_failures.txt. Any other failure fails CI, and the runner reports listed tests that now pass, to be removed from the list.

docs.title: Vendored and generated code
docs.text:
Many modules under python/pyspark are verbatim copies of PySpark 4.3.0, such as pyspark.pandas, pyspark.cloudpickle and much of pyspark.ml and pyspark.errors, and so is Spark's spatial reference system registry that the Rust crate embeds, crates/spark-connect/src/srs_registry.csv. Do not edit them: they are listed in scripts/check_vendored_upstream.sh (and the Python ones in the ruff excludes of pyproject.toml), and CI fails when one that the script lists differs from the v4.3.0 tag (the script fetches it from GitHub):

bash scripts/check_vendored_upstream.sh

Fix a behavior in the Rust core (crates/spark-connect), in the bindings (crates/pyspark-rs) or in a hand-written shim instead, and not by monkey-patching a Rust class from Python.

python/pyspark/sql/functions_generated.py and crates/pyspark-rs/src/dispatch_generated.rs are generated from crates/spark-connect/src/functions.rs. Regenerate them after changing a function there; CI runs the same command with --check:

python scripts/gen_fn_dispatch.py --pyspark-src "$SPARK_HOME/python"

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
cargo fmt --all                                         # format (CI runs it with --check)
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   # lint (blocking in CI)

Rust CI builds with RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings", so a compiler warning fails it, and so does any clippy finding. Clippy over the workspace needs the wasm32-unknown-unknown target (rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown), because it builds examples/wasm-udfs. CI runs rustfmt and clippy with a pinned toolchain, Rust 1.100.0 (.github/workflows/lint.yml), so that their verdicts do not change with a new release: run cargo +1.100.0 clippy ... to match it. CI also lints the datafusion and polars features of apache-spark-connect, and the crates that the workspace excludes (examples/wasm-udfs, examples/wasm-udf-inline and tests/wasm-udf) through their manifests. The lints this codebase triggers by design are allowed once, with a reason, in [workspace.lints.clippy] of the root Cargo.toml; a targeted #[allow] needs a comment saying why. CI also fails on deferral markers such as TODO, FIXME, todo!() or "for now" in crates/*/src (bash scripts/audit_no_stubs.sh). Match the surrounding code, keep changes focused, and add or update golden tests when you change plan or expression building.

Python is checked with ruff 0.14.0, the version CI pins, within the scope and excludes of pyproject.toml. Run it from the repository root without paths, as CI does:

ruff check
ruff format --check
python python/tests/test_ruff_excludes.py   # the excludes match the vendored list

ruff format covers scripts/ and the Row and value sources that the extension embeds: the shim and the tests are linted but not reformatted, so that open pull requests don't conflict. When you pass paths, for example from an editor, add --force-exclude: without it, ruff checks and formats every path it is given, vendored ones included.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text: Open PRs against apache/spark-connect-rust. Keep the PR description tied to its JIRA. Before you push, make sure cargo test and cargo fmt --all --check pass and, for a change to the drop-in, the offline Python tests and ruff; CI runs these as well as the end-to-end and official suites, coverage and the vendored-code check.

docs.title: Reading and Writing
docs.text: The spark_connect crate lets you read data from and write data to multiple file formats and data sources, with the server resolving all paths.

docs.title: Basic Read
docs.text:
Use spark.read() to access the DataFrameReader, specifying a format and path.

// Generic format API
let df = spark.read()
    .format("parquet")
    .load(Some("/path/to/file.parquet"));

// Shortcuts
let df = spark.read().parquet("/path/to/file.parquet");
let df = spark.read().csv("/path/to/file.csv");
let df = spark.read().json("/path/to/file.json");

docs.title: Common Read Options
docs.text:
Set read behavior with .option(key, value):

let df = spark.read()
    .format("csv")
    .option("header", "true")
    .option("delimiter", ",")
    .option("inferSchema", "true")
    .load(Some("/path/to/data.csv"));
Option Format Description header CSV First row contains column names delimiter CSV Field separator (default: comma) inferSchema CSV, JSON Auto-detect column types recursiveFileLookup Parquet, CSV, JSON Recursively search directories mode All PERMISSIVE, DROPMALFORMED, FAILFAST for error handling

docs.title: Supported Formats
docs.text:
• Parquet: Columnar format; default for DataFrames.
  • CSV: Delimiter-separated values; requires header option.
  • JSON: Line-delimited JSON objects.
  • ORC: Optimized columnar format.
  • Delta: Unified format with ACID transactions (Delta Lake).

docs.title: Basic Write
docs.text:
Use df.write() to access the DataFrameWriter, specifying a format and save location:

df.write()
    .format("parquet")
    .mode("overwrite")
    .save(Some("/path/to/output"))?;

// Shortcuts
df.write().parquet("/path/to/output.parquet")?;
df.write().csv("/path/to/output.csv")?;
df.write().json("/path/to/output.json")?;

docs.title: Save Modes
docs.text:
Control behavior when the target path already exists:

Mode Behavior overwrite Replace existing data append Add data to existing directory ignore Do nothing if path exists error Raise an error (default)

docs.title: Partitioning
docs.text:
Organize output by one or more columns:

df.write()
    .format("parquet")
    .partition_by(["year", "month"])
    .mode("overwrite")
    .save(Some("/path/to/output"))?;

docs.title: Catalog Tables
docs.text:
Save as a managed or external table:

df.write().mode("overwrite").save_as_table("my_table")?;
df.write()
    .mode("overwrite")
    .option("path", "/custom/path")
    .save_as_table("my_table")?;

Note

All file paths are resolved by the Spark Connect server, not the client. Ensure the server has access to the target location.

docs.title: DataFrames
docs.text: DataFrames are the core abstraction in Spark Connect-immutable, distributed tables. Create them from ranges, SQL, external data, or in-memory collections, then transform and aggregate them using a fluent API.

docs.title: Creating DataFrames
docs.text:
use spark_connect::SparkSession;

let spark = SparkSession::builder()
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .get_or_create()?;

// From a range
let df = spark.range(100)?;

// From SQL
let df = spark.sql("SELECT 1 as id")?;

// From external source (planned)
// let df = spark.read().parquet("path/to/file.parquet")?;

// From in-memory data (planned)
// let df = spark.create_data_frame(...)?;

Note

Remote session requires a Spark Connect server running at sc://localhost:15002.

docs.title: Transformations
docs.text:
Transform DataFrames with chainable operations like select, filter, and with_column.

use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit};

// Select columns
let df = df.select([f::col("id"), f::col("name")]);

// Filter rows
let df = df.filter(f::col("id").gt(lit(10)));

// Add/modify column
let df = df.with_column("double_id", f::col("id") * lit(2));

// Rename column
let df = df.with_column_renamed("id", "row_id");

// Drop columns
let df = df.drop(vec!["temp_col"]);

// Distinct rows
let df = df.distinct();

// Sort
let df = df.order_by([f::col("id")]);

// Limit
let df = df.limit(5);

docs.title: Grouping and Aggregation
docs.text:
Group rows and compute aggregates like count, sum, and average.

use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit};

// Group by one column
let agg_df = df.group_by([f::col("category")])
    .agg([f::count(lit(1))]);

// Group by multiple columns with multiple aggregates
let agg_df = df.group_by([f::col("category"), f::col("year")])
    .agg([
        f::sum(f::col("amount")),
        f::avg(f::col("value")),
        f::min(f::col("price")).alias("min_price"),
    ]);

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
Combine DataFrames on shared keys.

use spark_connect::{functions as f, plan::JoinType};

// Inner join (default)
let joined = df1.join(
    &df2,
    Some(f::col("df1.id").eq(f::col("df2.id"))),
    JoinType::Inner,
);

// Left outer join
let joined = df1.join(&df2, Some(f::col("id").eq(f::col("id"))), JoinType::LeftOuter);

// Cross join
let crossed = df1.join(&df2, None, JoinType::Cross);

docs.title: Set Operations
docs.text:
Combine or deduplicate across DataFrames.

// Union (stacks rows, allows duplicates)
let combined = df1.union(&df2);

// Union by name (aligns columns)
let combined = df1.union_by_name(&df2);

// Except (rows in df1 not in df2)
let diff = df1.except_all(&df2);

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Execute and retrieve results.

// Display first n rows
df.show(10)?;

// Collect all rows to driver
let rows = df.collect()?;

// Count rows
let count = df.count()?;

// Get first n rows
let first_rows = df.take(5)?;

// Get first row
let first = df.first()?;

docs.title: Example Pipeline
docs.text:
use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit};

let result = spark.range(101)?
    .with_column("squared", f::col("id") * f::col("id"))
    .filter(f::col("squared").gt(lit(100)))
    .select([f::col("id"), f::col("squared")])
    .order_by([f::col("id")])
    .limit(10);
result.show(10)?;

Tip

See Columns and Functions for expression building, SQL for SQL queries, and Reading and Writing for I/O.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Curated recipes for common Spark Connect tasks. See the repository's examples/ directory for more runnable Rust examples.

docs.title: Read and Aggregate CSV
docs.text:
Read a CSV file and compute summary statistics:

use spark_connect::functions as f;

let df = spark.read()
    .format("csv")
    .option("header", "true")
    .option("inferSchema", "true")
    .load(Some("data.csv"));

df
    .group_by([f::col("category")])
    .agg([f::sum(f::col("amount")), f::avg(f::col("price"))])
    .show(20)?;

docs.title: Word Count
docs.text:
Classic MapReduce-style word count over a text column:

use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit_string};

let df = spark.sql(
    "SELECT * FROM VALUES ('hello world'), ('hello spark') AS t(line)"
)?;

df
    .select([f::explode(
        f::split(f::col("line"), lit_string(" "))
    ).alias("word")])
    .group_by([f::col("word")])
    .agg([f::count(f::col("word"))])
    .show(20)?;

docs.title: Join Two DataFrames
docs.text:
Join two DataFrames on a common key:

use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit, plan::JoinType};

let users = spark.range(2)?
    .with_column("name", f::col("id"));
let orders = spark.range(3)?
    .with_column("user_id", f::col("id"))
    .with_column("amount", lit(100));

users
    .join(&orders, Some(f::col("id").eq(f::col("user_id"))), JoinType::Inner)
    .select([f::col("name"), f::col("amount")])
    .show(20)?;

docs.title: Write Parquet
docs.text:
Save a DataFrame to Parquet format:

let df = spark.range(1000)?;
df.write()
    .mode("overwrite")
    .format("parquet")
    .save(Some("/tmp/output"))?;

docs.title: SQL Query
docs.text:
Run a SQL query directly:

let df = spark.range(100)?;
df.create_or_replace_temp_view("numbers")?;

spark
    .sql("SELECT * FROM numbers WHERE id > 50")?
    .show(20)?;

docs.title: More Examples
docs.text: Explore the repository's examples/ directory for additional runnable examples, including streaming, complex transformations, and integration with external data sources.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Add the Spark Connect Rust client to your project. The native Rust crate is the primary library; Python support is a drop-in replacement for PySpark.

docs.title: Rust (Native Crate)
docs.text:
Add the crate to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
apache-spark-connect = "4.3"

docs.title: Optional Features
docs.text:
Enable optional features for additional functionality:

[dependencies]
apache-spark-connect = { version = "4.3", features = ["datafusion", "polars"] }

Requirements: - Rust 1.88 or later (1.94 or later with the datafusion feature) - protobuf-compiler (e.g., brew install protobuf on macOS, apt-get install protobuf-compiler on Linux) - A running Spark Connect server (see Configuration and Connection)

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
To build the native library locally:

git clone https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust
cd spark-connect-rust
cargo build --release

Build requirements: - Rust toolchain (rustup / cargo) - protobuf-compiler - For non-Windows aarch64 targets, a C compiler/assembler and archiver that support the target, required by sha2-asm. Install build-essential on Debian/Ubuntu or Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS. Cross-compilation needs the corresponding target tools, configured for the cc crate (for example, through its target-specific CC_<target> and AR_<target> variables).

docs.title: Python (Drop-in Replacement)
docs.text: pyspark-client-rust is a faster, drop-in replacement for the official pyspark Spark Connect client on PyPI. It uses the same pyspark import path and public API, but executes plan building, transport, and Arrow decoding in Rust for better performance.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
All three PyPI packages that ship a Spark Connect client - pyspark, pyspark-client, and pyspark-client-rust - install into the same pyspark import directory, so only one can be active in an environment at a time. Do not install pyspark-client-rust on top of another one: pip does not remove the previous distribution's files first, so you would be left with a mix of both and a broken pyspark. Always uninstall the existing client first:

pip uninstall -y pyspark pyspark-client
pip install pyspark-client-rust

Switching back to the reference client

For the same reason, uninstalling pyspark-client-rust is not enough to restore the reference client - it removes the shared pyspark files and leaves the environment with no working pyspark. Reinstall PySpark explicitly afterward:

pip uninstall -y pyspark-client-rust
pip install pyspark-client   # or `pyspark` for full Apache Spark

Requirements: - Python 3.9 or later - A running Spark Connect server

docs.title: Usage and API Reference
docs.text:
Use it exactly like PySpark. For the complete Python API reference, see the official PySpark documentation.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()

docs.title: Build from Source (Python)
docs.text:
To build and install the Python wheel:

pip install maturin
maturin build --release --out dist
pip install dist/pyspark_client_rust-*.whl

Build requirements: - Python 3.9 or later - Rust toolchain (rustup / cargo) - protobuf-compiler - For non-Windows aarch64 targets, the C toolchain described in the Rust source build requirements.

Installing a prebuilt Python wheel does not require a C toolchain.

docs.title: Version and Compatibility
docs.text: The crate and package versions track Apache Spark: version 4.3.x supports Spark 4.3.0 and later. The wire protocol is identical to the reference client, so existing Spark Connect code works unchanged.

docs.text:

  • Configuration and Connection - connect to a remote or local Spark Connect server

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Get up and running with Spark Connect in minutes. This guide walks you through your first Rust query.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you start, ensure you have a running Spark Connect server. See Configuration and Connection for how to start one locally:

$SPARK_HOME/sbin/start-connect-server.sh

The server listens on sc://localhost:15002 by default.

docs.title: Your First Query
docs.text:
Connect to the server and run a simple query:

use spark_connect::SparkSession;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let spark = SparkSession::builder()
        .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
        .get_or_create()?;

    let df = spark.range(10)?;
    df.show(20)?;
    println!("Count: {}", df.count()?);

    Ok(())
}

docs.title: Filtering and Selection
docs.text:
Add a filter and select specific columns:

use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit};

let df = spark.range(100)?;
df
    .filter(f::col("id").gt(lit(50)))
    .select([f::col("id")])
    .show(20)?;

docs.title: Aggregation and Grouping
docs.text:
Compute aggregations over grouped data:

use spark_connect::{functions as f, lit};

let df = spark.range(20)?;
df
    .with_column("category", f::col("id") % lit(3))
    .group_by([f::col("category")])
    .agg([
        f::sum(f::col("id")).alias("total"),
        f::avg(f::col("id")).alias("average"),
    ])
    .show(20)?;

docs.title: Using it from an async runtime
docs.text: The API is synchronous and can be called from any thread, including inside a Tokio runtime of either flavor. The call blocks the thread it runs on until the server answers, so keep it out of tasks that must keep the rest of their runtime running. A current_thread runtime, such as the one of #[tokio::test], works too: the query runs on a thread of its own while the calling thread waits, and it keeps the tags and user context extensions of the calling thread.

docs.title: SQL
docs.text: Execute SQL directly against DataFrames and data sources. Mix SQL queries with the DataFrame API for maximum flexibility.

docs.title: Running SQL Queries
docs.text:
Use spark.sql() to execute SQL and retrieve results as a DataFrame.

use spark_connect::SparkSession;

let spark = SparkSession::builder()
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .get_or_create()?;

// Simple query
let df = spark.sql("SELECT 1 as id, 'hello' as msg")?;
df.show(10)?;

// Aggregate query
let df = spark.sql(
    r#"SELECT category, COUNT(*) as cnt, AVG(price) as avg_price
       FROM products
       GROUP BY category
       ORDER BY cnt DESC"#
)?;
df.show(10)?;

docs.title: Registering Temporary Views
docs.text:
Make DataFrames queryable via SQL by creating temporary views.

use spark_connect::SparkSession;

let spark = SparkSession::builder()
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .get_or_create()?;

// Create from range
let df = spark.range(4)?;

// Register as temp view
df.create_or_replace_temp_view("users")?;

// Query it
let result = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id > 1")?;
result.show(10)?;

// Replace view
let df_updated = spark.sql("SELECT id FROM users")?;
df_updated.create_or_replace_temp_view("users")?;

Note

Temporary views are scoped to the session and are dropped when the session ends.

docs.title: Dynamic values
docs.text:
SparkSession::sql takes a single query string; there is no server-side parameter-binding API. For caller-controlled values, prefer the typed DataFrame API rather than splicing them into SQL text -- values are passed as literals, so untrusted input cannot break the query or inject SQL:

use spark_connect::{SparkSession, functions as f, lit, lit_string};

let spark = SparkSession::builder()
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .get_or_create()?;

let threshold = 50;
let category = "electronics";

// Injection-safe: the values are literals, not part of the SQL string.
let df = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM products")?
    .filter(f::col("price").gt(lit(threshold)))
    .filter(f::col("category").eq(lit_string(category)));

Warning

Building a query by interpolation (format!) is not injection-safe and must only be used with trusted, validated input:

// Trusted input only - NOT safe for user-controlled values.
let threshold = 50;
let df = spark.sql(&format!("SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > {}", threshold))?;

docs.title: Mixing SQL and DataFrames
docs.text:
Alternate between SQL queries and DataFrame API transformations.

use spark_connect::{SparkSession, functions as f, lit};

// Start with SQL
let raw = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM raw_data")?;

// Transform with DataFrame API
let cleaned = raw
    .filter(f::col("value").gt(lit(0)))
    .select([f::col("id"), f::col("value")])
    .with_column("scaled", f::col("value") * lit(2));

// Register result for SQL
cleaned.create_or_replace_temp_view("cleaned_data")?;

// Query it with SQL
let aggregated = spark.sql(
    r#"SELECT id, COUNT(*) as cnt, AVG(scaled) as avg_scaled
       FROM cleaned_data
       GROUP BY id"#
)?;
aggregated.show(10)?;

docs.title: SQL and DataFrame Interop Example
docs.text:
use spark_connect::{SparkSession, functions as f, lit, lit_string};
use spark_connect::column::when; // CASE/WHEN builder (supports `.otherwise`)

// Create test data (from range with derived columns)
let df = spark.range(5)?
    .with_column(
        "category",
        when(f::col("id").le(lit(2)), lit_string("Electronics"))
            .otherwise(lit_string("Books"))
    )
    .with_column(
        "price",
        when(f::col("id").eq(lit(1)), lit(299))
            .when(f::col("id").eq(lit(2)), lit(150))
            .when(f::col("id").eq(lit(3)), lit(25))
            .otherwise(lit(30))
    );
df.create_or_replace_temp_view("products")?;

// SQL: aggregate by category
let by_cat = spark.sql(
    r#"SELECT category, COUNT(*) as count, AVG(price) as avg_price
       FROM products
       GROUP BY category"#
)?;
by_cat.create_or_replace_temp_view("category_stats")?;

// DataFrame API: filter and order
let result = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM category_stats")?
    .filter(f::col("avg_price").gt(lit(50)))
    .order_by([f::col("count").desc()]);
result.show(10)?;

Tip

Temporary views make it easy to break complex transformations into readable steps. See DataFrames for more on the API, and Catalog for managing tables and schemas.

docs.title: Structured Streaming
docs.text: The spark_connect crate supports Structured Streaming for continuous data processing from streaming sources and sinks.

docs.title: Reading Streams
docs.text:
Use spark.read_stream() to create a streaming DataFrame:

// Rate source (generates rows at specified rate; useful for testing)
let df = spark.read_stream()
    .format("rate")
    .option("rowsPerSecond", "10")
    .load(None);

// File source (monitors directory for new files)
let df = spark.read_stream()
    .format("csv")
    .option("header", "true")
    .schema("value string")
    .load(Some("/path/to/stream/input"));

docs.title: Stream Transformations
docs.text:
Apply SQL operations on streaming DataFrames as you would on static ones:

use spark_connect::{col, lit};

let result = df
    .filter(col("value").gt(lit(10)))
    .select([col("timestamp"), col("value")])
    .write_stream()
    .format("console")
    .start("")?;

docs.title: Writing Streams
docs.text:
Use df.write_stream() to write a streaming DataFrame to a sink:

use spark_connect::streaming::Trigger;

// Console sink
let query = df.write_stream()
    .format("console")
    .output_mode("append")
    .trigger(Trigger::ProcessingTime("5 seconds".to_string()))
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/checkpoint")
    .start("")?;

// Memory sink (debug only; stores in table)
let query = df.write_stream()
    .format("memory")
    .query_name("my_stream")
    .output_mode("append")
    .start("")?;

// File sink (Parquet)
let query = df.write_stream()
    .format("parquet")
    .output_mode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/checkpoint")
    .start("/path/to/output")?;

docs.title: Output Modes
docs.text: Mode Behavior append Add new rows to sink only complete Rewrite entire result set (aggregations only) update Update changed rows only (aggregations only)

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
Control how often results are written:

  • trigger("processingTime=5 seconds") - Write every 5 seconds.
  • trigger("once=true") - Process one micro-batch then stop.
  • trigger("continuous=1 second") - Continuous mode (lower latency).

docs.title: Awaiting Termination
docs.text:
Block until a query stops (either by error or stop()):

let query = df.write_stream().format("console").start("")?;
query.await_termination(None)?;

docs.title: Stopping a Query
docs.text:
Gracefully stop a streaming query:

query.stop()?;

docs.title: Active Queries
docs.text:
List all active streaming queries in the session:

for q in spark.streams().active()? {
    println!("Query {}: {:?}", q.id(), q.is_active()?);
}

Warning

Checkpoints are mandatory for fault tolerance. Always set checkpointLocation for production queries.

docs.title: Listener failures
docs.text:
For native Rust listeners, a terminal stream end or error clears the subscription's registrations. The default StreamingQueryListener::on_stream_error hook is silent; override it to report failures, and re-add listeners to open a new subscription. A normal stream end clears registrations without calling the error hook. Adapters can return errors through try_on_event or provide shared asynchronous dispatch through try_post_to_all. Use DataStreamWriter::start_with_event_handler or to_table_with_event_handler for shared synchronous start-event decoding.

SparkSession::stop() and close() cancel listener dispatch and clear registrations locally, without sending a listener-removal RPC or joining callbacks already running. Reference PySpark leaves listener-bus cleanup to its handler thread during session stop.

The PySpark drop-in listener bus deserializes each event once before invoking callbacks and shares that event object across all listener registrations. A malformed start event raises from start() or toTable(), even when no listeners are registered. A transport failure, malformed asynchronous event or unknown event type warns and clears the subscription's listeners. Add the listeners again to open a subscription. A server-side end of the event stream also clears registrations without a warning; reference PySpark retains them after a normal stream end.

streams.close() removes every listener. Reference PySpark's close() removes the listeners while it iterates over its list, which each removal shortens, so with three listeners it leaves the second one registered, with the server's listener. The drop-in does not mirror that.

Callback exceptions derived from Exception produce per-listener warnings and dispatch continues. An uncaught BaseException, or a callback warning promoted to an error by Python's warning filters, terminates the native subscription and clears its registrations. This cleanup is deliberate: reference PySpark can retain stale registrations when its handler exits through BaseException. The terminal handler warning is best effort when warning filters themselves raise errors.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues and solutions when using Spark Connect Rust.

docs.title: Cannot Connect to Server / Connection Refused
docs.text:
Symptom: Error: Failed to connect to sc://localhost:15002 or connection timeout.

Solution: 1. Verify the server is running: $SPARK_HOME/sbin/start-connect-server.sh 2. Check the port is correct. By default it's 15002. To verify, look for spark.connect.grpc.binding.port in the server logs. 3. If connecting to a remote server, verify network connectivity: ping spark.example.com and check firewalls. 4. Ensure Apache Spark 4.3.0 or later is installed: $SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-shell --version

Tip

Run the server in the foreground to see startup messages: SPARK_NO_DAEMONIZE=1 $SPARK_HOME/sbin/start-connect-server.sh

docs.title: TLS / Authentication Error
docs.text:
Symptom: Error: TLS handshake failed or UNAUTHENTICATED error when connecting.

Solution: 1. Verify you are using the correct connection string format with TLS enabled: 

use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
    .remote("sc://host:15002/;use_ssl=true;token=YOUR_TOKEN")
    .get_or_create()?;
2. If the server uses self-signed certificates, consult your infrastructure team. 3. Check that your token or authentication credentials are valid. 4. Verify the server is configured to accept your authentication method (check server config or logs).

Note

Authentication parameters are passed in the connection string, not as config options.

docs.title: Slow First Query / Long Session Startup
docs.text:
Symptom: The first query takes 10–30 seconds, or SparkSession creation is slow.

Solution: This is normal. The JVM and Spark runtime warm up on first use. Subsequent queries are fast.

  • If this is unacceptable for your use case, consider keeping a long-lived session and reusing it.
  • Profile your workload: most of the overhead is in JVM startup, not the Rust client.
  • On a remote server, network latency may add to startup time.

docs.title: Protobuf Compilation Error
docs.text:
Symptom: Error during cargo build: protobuf compiler not found or similar.

Solution: 1. Install protobuf-compiler: - macOS: brew install protobuf - Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): apt-get install protobuf-compiler - Other systems: See Protocol Buffers documentation 2. Verify installation: protoc --version 3. Retry: cargo build --release

docs.title: Dataset Version Mismatch
docs.text:
Symptom: Errors about incompatible schema or unexpected null values.

Solution: 1. Verify the Spark Connect server and client are compatible versions: both should be Spark 4.3.0 or later. 2. If you recently upgraded Apache Spark, restart the Spark Connect server to apply the new version. 3. Check that data on disk matches the expected schema (e.g., after schema changes, re-write the data).

docs.title: Types and Schemas
docs.text: Spark SQL uses a rich type system. Learn how to work with schemas in the spark_connect crate and cast columns between types.

docs.title: Spark SQL Types
docs.text:
Each Spark SQL type is a variant of the spark_connect::types::DataType enum, which is also exported as spark_connect::DataType. The tables below give, for each type:

  • DDL: how a DDL string writes the type, which is also its simple_string(). DataType::from_ddl and the server parse this and the aliases in parentheses.
  • DataType: the Rust value of the type.
  • Collected as: the spark_connect::row::Value that collect() gives for a value of the type in a Row.

A NULL of any type is collected as Value::Null.

docs.title: Numbers and booleans
docs.text:
Spark type DDL DataType Collected as BooleanType boolean DataType::Boolean Value::Bool(bool) ByteType tinyint (byte) DataType::Byte Value::Byte(i8) ShortType smallint (short) DataType::Short Value::Short(i16) IntegerType int (integer) DataType::Integer Value::Integer(i32) LongType bigint (long) DataType::Long Value::Long(i64) FloatType float (real) DataType::Float Value::Float(f32) DoubleType double DataType::Double Value::Double(f64) DecimalType decimal(10,2) (dec, numeric) DataType::Decimal { precision: 10, scale: 2 } Value::Decimal { value, precision, scale }

A decimal is collected exactly, as text: CAST(1.5 AS DECIMAL(10,2)) is Value::Decimal { value: "1.50", precision: Some(10), scale: Some(2) }. In DDL, a bare decimal is decimal(10,0) and decimal(p) is decimal(p,0).

docs.title: Strings and binary
docs.text:
Spark type DDL DataType Collected as StringType string DataType::String { collation: "UTF8_BINARY".to_string() } Value::String(String) StringType with a collation string collate UTF8_LCASE DataType::String { collation: "UTF8_LCASE".to_string() } Value::String(String) CharType char(5) (character(5)) DataType::Char { length: 5 } Value::String(String) VarcharType varchar(10) DataType::Varchar { length: 10 } Value::String(String) BinaryType binary DataType::Binary Value::Binary(Vec<u8>)

collation names the collation of a string, which decides how strings compare. UTF8_BINARY is the default, and simple_string() leaves it out; any other, such as UTF8_LCASE, UNICODE or UNICODE_CI, is written string collate <name>. from_ddl gives the name in the case that the server uses, so string collate unicode_ci has the collation UNICODE_CI. In the JSON of a struct field (json()), the collations of its strings are in the __COLLATIONS entry of the field's metadata, where Spark writes them.

A cast to char(5) or varchar(5) gives a string column, with no padding and no length check, unless the session sets spark.sql.preserveCharVarcharTypeInfo to true: then the column keeps DataType::Char or DataType::Varchar, and a CHAR value is padded to its length. The server rejects CHAR and VARCHAR in the schema of create_dataframe and of DataFrameReader::schema with UNSUPPORTED_CHAR_OR_VARCHAR_AS_STRING, even with that setting; use string there.

docs.title: Dates, times and timestamps
docs.text:
Spark type DDL DataType Collected as DateType date DataType::Date Value::Date(i32): days since 1970-01-01 TimestampType timestamp (timestamp_ltz) DataType::Timestamp Value::Timestamp(i64): microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC TimestampNTZType timestamp_ntz DataType::TimestampNtz Value::TimestampNtz(i64): microseconds of the date-time since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 TimeType time(6) (time) DataType::Time { precision: 6 } Value::Time(i64): nanoseconds since midnight TimestampNTZNanosType timestamp_ntz(9) DataType::TimestampNtzNanos { precision: 9 } Value::TimestampNtz(i64), in microseconds TimestampLTZNanosType timestamp_ltz(9) (timestamp(9)) DataType::TimestampLtzNanos { precision: 9 } Value::Timestamp(i64), in microseconds

A Value::Timestamp is an instant: TIMESTAMP'2024-01-02 03:04:05.123456' is Value::Timestamp(1704164645123456) when the session time zone (spark.sql.session.timeZone) is UTC, and the time zone only decides which instant a literal or a string means. A Value::TimestampNtz is a date-time that no time zone shifts. from_ddl always reads timestamp as DataType::Timestamp, while the server reads it as DataType::TimestampNtz when spark.sql.timestampType is TIMESTAMP_NTZ; SparkSession::parse_ddl parses a DDL string on the server, as the server reads it.

A TIME has a precision of 0 to 9 fractional digits, and time is time(6). A value is collected in nanoseconds: TIME'12:34:56.123456' is Value::Time(45296123456000). Spark 4.3 supports TIME only when spark.sql.timeType.enabled is true, which is not its default; otherwise a query of a TIME fails with UNSUPPORTED_TIME_TYPE.

timestamp_ntz(p) and timestamp_ltz(p) with a precision p of 7 to 9 are the nanosecond timestamps, a preview in Spark 4.3: timestamp(p) is timestamp_ltz(p), while timestamp(6) and timestamp_ntz(6) are the microsecond types. The server takes them only when spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled is true, which is not its default and which a session can set with spark.conf().set(...); otherwise it fails with FEATURE_NOT_ENABLED. collect gives them in microseconds, in the Value variants of the microsecond types, rounding the sub-microsecond digits down; DataFrame::to_arrow keeps the nanoseconds.

docs.title: Intervals
docs.text:
Spark type DDL DataType Collected as YearMonthIntervalType interval year to month (interval year, interval month) DataType::YearMonthInterval { start_field: 0, end_field: 1 } Value::YearMonthInterval(i32): months DayTimeIntervalType interval day to second (interval day, interval hour to minute, ...) DataType::DayTimeInterval { start_field: 0, end_field: 3 } Value::DayTimeInterval(i64): microseconds CalendarIntervalType interval DataType::CalendarInterval Value::String(String), as "1 months 2 days 11045500000000 ns"

start_field and end_field are the first and the last field of an interval: YearMonthIntervalType::YEAR (0) and MONTH (1), or DayTimeIntervalType::DAY (0), HOUR (1), MINUTE (2) and SECOND (3). INTERVAL '1-2' YEAR TO MONTH is collected as Value::YearMonthInterval(14), and INTERVAL '1 02:03:04.5' DAY TO SECOND as Value::DayTimeInterval(93784500000). create_dataframe takes these values for interval year to month and interval day to second columns; the server rejects them for the narrower interval types, such as interval year or interval hour to minute, with INVALID_COLUMN_OR_FIELD_DATA_TYPE.

interval alone is the calendar interval, of months, days and microseconds, that functions such as make_interval return. It has no Value variant: it is collected as the text of its months, days and nanoseconds, and create_dataframe cannot take it.

docs.title: Arrays, maps and structs
docs.text:
Spark type DDL DataType Collected as ArrayType array<int> DataType::Array { element_type: Box::new(DataType::Integer), contains_null: true } Value::List(Vec<Value>) MapType map<string,int> DataType::Map { key_type, value_type, value_contains_null } Value::Map(Vec<(Value, Value)>), its entries in order StructType struct<a:int,b:string> DataType::Struct { fields }, of StructFields Value::Struct(StructValue), its names and values in order

DDL does not say whether the elements of an array or the values of a map may be null: from_ddl gives contains_null: true and value_contains_null: true. A struct field is nullable unless it is NOT NULL. See Nested Types.

docs.title: Variant and spatial types
docs.text:
Spark type DDL DataType Collected as VariantType variant DataType::Variant Value::Variant { value, metadata }, both Vec<u8> GeometryType geometry(4326) (geometry(any)) DataType::Geometry { srid: 4326 } Value::Struct of srid (Value::Integer) and wkb (Value::Binary) GeographyType geography(4326) (geography(any)) DataType::Geography { srid: 4326 } Value::Struct of srid and wkb

A variant is collected as the two binary parts of Spark's variant encoding, which this crate does not decode. To read one as JSON, select to_json of it on the server.

A spatial type has the SRID of the spatial reference system of its values, or allows any SRID, which is srid: -1 (SpatialType::MIXED_SRID) and any in DDL. A value is collected as a struct of its SRID and its WKB (well-known binary) geometry, and create_dataframe takes the same struct. from_ddl reads the SRID as Spark's parser does, of digits or any: an SRID that the type does not take, such as 99999, or a geography of 3857, is ST_INVALID_SRID_VALUE, and another argument, such as -1, +5 or a CRS (EPSG:2154), is not one of Spark's grammar, so it is an INVALID_DATATYPE_FORMAT error, where the server's parser raises PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR.

The SRIDs are those of Spark's spatial reference system registry (about 10,700 systems, embedded from Spark's srs_registry.csv). A geometry takes any of them, and a geography only a geographic one. The JSON of a spatial type (json()) names its reference system by the string ID that Spark writes: geometry(OGC:CRS84) is SRID 4326, geometry(EPSG:2154) is SRID 2154 and geometry(SRID:0) is SRID 0; a geography also names its algorithm, as geography(OGC:CRS83, SPHERICAL) for SRID 4269. DataType::from_json and the server read these back, and the aliases of the OGC systems, such as EPSG:4269, too. As Spark's JSON reader, from_json reads a bare geometry and geography, and a geography of its algorithm alone (geography(SPHERICAL)), as of OGC:CRS84. The algorithm is SPHERICAL of any case, and another one is ST_INVALID_ALGORITHM_VALUE. A CRS is of the form <authority>:<code>, and one that Spark does not know, or that the type does not take, is ST_INVALID_CRS_VALUE. The SRIDs and the any of DDL, as geometry(4326), are not JSON. DDL, and the protobuf form in which the server sends a schema, carry any SRID.

The drop-in is stricter, as PySpark 4.3.0 is: its GeometryType takes the SRIDs 0, 3857 and 4326, and its GeographyType 4326, and it reads only the CRS names that those take, and the algorithm SPHERICAL only in upper case. A schema of the server with another SRID raises ST_INVALID_SRID_VALUE wherever PySpark converts the schema, also of a type nested in an array, a map or a struct: df.schema, columns, dtypes, repr(df), printSchema(), the collecting APIs (collect, toPandas, toArrow, ...) and a DDL schema, which the server parses. count and show read no schema, and work.

docs.title: Other types
docs.text:
Spark type DDL DataType Collected as NullType void DataType::Null Value::Null UserDefinedType (simple_string() is udt) DataType::Udt { .. } the Value of its SQL type A type for the server to parse (holds a DDL type string) DataType::Unparsed { data_type_string } (the server returns the parsed type)

A user-defined type, such as the vector type of Spark ML, is in a schema as DataType::Udt, with its JVM and Python classes (jvm_class: Some("org.apache.spark.ml.linalg.VectorUDT")), and its values are collected as those of its SQL type: a vector is a Value::Struct of type, size, indices and values.

DataType::Unparsed sends a DDL type string as it is, for the server to parse, wherever a DataType is sent: col("x").cast(DataType::Unparsed { data_type_string: "decimal(5,2)".to_string() }) casts to decimal(5,2). create_dataframe cannot take it.

Python drop-in

In the Python drop-in, pyspark.sql.types has PySpark's type classes (IntegerType(), StructType, ...), backed by this same DataType; see the PySpark documentation.

docs.title: Inspecting Schemas
docs.text:
DataFrame::schema returns the schema of a DataFrame as a DataType::Struct, whose StructFields have the name, type and nullability of each column:

use spark_connect::types::DataType;

let df = spark.sql(
    "SELECT 1L AS id, CAST(2.5 AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS price, \
     INTERVAL '1-2' YEAR TO MONTH AS term, array(named_struct('k', 'a', 'v', 1)) AS kv",
)?;

// Get full schema
if let DataType::Struct { fields } = df.schema()? {
    for field in &fields {
        // A DataType displays as its simple string: "bigint", "decimal(10,2)", ...
        println!("{}: {} (nullable = {})", field.name, field.data_type, field.nullable);
    }
}

// Column names: ["id", "price", "term", "kv"]
let names = df.columns()?;

// (name, type) pairs: [("id", "bigint"), ("price", "decimal(10,2)"), ...]
let dtypes = df.dtypes()?;
for (name, dtype) in dtypes {
    println!("{}: {}", name, dtype);
}

// Print schema
df.print_schema()?;

print_schema prints the schema as a tree, as DataType::tree_string gives it:

root
 |-- id: long (nullable = false)
 |-- price: decimal(10,2) (nullable = false)
 |-- term: interval year to month (nullable = false)
 |-- kv: array (nullable = false)
 |    |-- element: struct (containsNull = false)
 |    |    |-- k: string (nullable = false)
 |    |    |-- v: integer (nullable = false)

A DataType has the string forms of PySpark's types:

Method Gives Example simple_string(), also to_string() the DDL form, which dtypes shows bigint, array<struct<k:string,v:int>> type_name() PySpark's typeName(), which print_schema shows for most types long, array json() Spark's JSON form, which DataType::from_json_str parses "long" to_ddl() the DDL of the fields of a struct id BIGINT NOT NULL,price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,...

docs.title: Building a Schema
docs.text:
Define a schema explicitly when reading or creating DataFrames. A reader takes a DDL string, or the JSON of a DataType from json():

let df = spark
    .read()
    .schema("name string, age int, salary bigint".to_string())
    .csv("/path/to/data.csv");

DataType::from_ddl parses a DDL string into a DataType without the server, and a list of fields becomes a DataType::Struct. NOT NULL makes a field non-nullable, and COMMENT 'text' puts the text in the field's metadata under comment. create_dataframe takes the rows of a DataFrame and its schema: each Row has one Value for each field, in the order of the fields.

use spark_connect::row::{Row, Value};
use spark_connect::types::DataType;

let schema = DataType::from_ddl(
    "id bigint NOT NULL, amount decimal(10,2), wait interval day to second, \
     note string COMMENT 'free text'",
)?;

let rows = vec![Row::new(
    vec!["id".into(), "amount".into(), "wait".into(), "note".into()],
    vec![
        Value::Long(1),
        Value::Decimal {
            value: "12.50".into(),
            precision: Some(10),
            scale: Some(2),
        },
        // 1 hour 30 minutes, in microseconds
        Value::DayTimeInterval(90 * 60 * 1_000_000),
        Value::String("first".into()),
    ],
)];
let df = spark.create_dataframe(rows, schema)?;

A schema can also be built in Rust, with DataType::Struct and StructField (see Nested Types), or with add, which returns the struct with one more field:

use spark_connect::types::{DataType, DayTimeIntervalType};

let schema = DataType::Struct { fields: vec![] }
    .add("id", DataType::Long, false, None)?
    .add(
        "code",
        DataType::String {
            collation: "UTF8_LCASE".to_string(),
        },
        true,
        None,
    )?
    .add(
        "wait",
        DataType::DayTimeInterval {
            start_field: DayTimeIntervalType::DAY,
            end_field: DayTimeIntervalType::SECOND,
        },
        true,
        None,
    )?;

assert_eq!(
    schema,
    DataType::from_ddl(
        "id bigint NOT NULL, code string collate UTF8_LCASE, wait interval day to second"
    )?
);

docs.title: Casting Columns
docs.text:
Convert a column to a different type with .cast():

use spark_connect::{col, types::DataType};

// Cast to LongType
let df = df.with_column("id", col("id").cast(DataType::Long));

// Cast to DoubleType
let df = df.with_column("price", col("price").cast(DataType::Double));

// Cast with a type name string
let df = df.with_column("created", col("created").cast_str("timestamp"));

cast_str sends the type string for the server to parse, so "timestamp" is TIMESTAMP_NTZ there when spark.sql.timestampType is TIMESTAMP_NTZ. try_cast and try_cast_str give NULL for a value that cannot be cast, where cast fails the query in ANSI mode, Spark's default:

use spark_connect::{
    col,
    types::{DataType, DayTimeIntervalType},
};

let df = spark.sql("SELECT '1 02:03:04.5' AS wait, 'abc' AS n")?;

// To an interval day to second: Value::DayTimeInterval(93784500000)
let df = df.with_column(
    "wait",
    col("wait").cast(DataType::DayTimeInterval {
        start_field: DayTimeIntervalType::DAY,
        end_field: DayTimeIntervalType::SECOND,
    }),
);

// "abc" is not a number, so this is NULL, while cast(DataType::Integer) fails
let df = df.with_column("n", col("n").try_cast(DataType::Integer));

docs.title: Nested Types
docs.text:
Work with complex nested structures:

use spark_connect::types::{DataType, StructField};
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

// Array of strings
let array_of_strings = DataType::Array {
    element_type: Box::new(DataType::String {
        collation: "UTF8_BINARY".to_string(),
    }),
    contains_null: true,
};

// Map with string keys and integer values
let map_type = DataType::Map {
    key_type: Box::new(DataType::String {
        collation: "UTF8_BINARY".to_string(),
    }),
    value_type: Box::new(DataType::Integer),
    value_contains_null: true,
};

// Nested struct
let nested = DataType::Struct {
    fields: vec![
        StructField {
            name: "name".to_string(),
            data_type: DataType::String {
                collation: "UTF8_BINARY".to_string(),
            },
            nullable: true,
            metadata: BTreeMap::new(),
        },
        StructField {
            name: "tags".to_string(),
            data_type: DataType::Array {
                element_type: Box::new(DataType::String {
                    collation: "UTF8_BINARY".to_string(),
                }),
                contains_null: true,
            },
            nullable: true,
            metadata: BTreeMap::new(),
        },
    ],
};

// The same types in DDL
assert_eq!(array_of_strings, DataType::from_ddl("array<string>")?);
assert_eq!(map_type, DataType::from_ddl("map<string,int>")?);
assert_eq!(nested, DataType::from_ddl("struct<name:string,tags:array<string>>")?);

Note

Nullable fields allow NULL values. Set nullable to false when a field must always have a value. contains_null and value_contains_null do the same for the elements of an array and the values of a map.

Nested values are collected as Value::List, Value::Map and Value::Struct; the fields of a struct can be read by name or by position:

use spark_connect::row::Value;

let rows = spark
    .sql("SELECT named_struct('name', 'a', 'tags', array('x', 'y')) AS s, map('k', 1) AS m")?
    .collect()?;

if let Some(Value::Struct(s)) = rows[0].get_by_name("s") {
    assert_eq!(s.get_by_name("name"), Some(&Value::String("a".into())));
    if let Some(Value::List(tags)) = s.get(1) {
        assert_eq!(tags, &vec![Value::String("x".into()), Value::String("y".into())]);
    }
}
if let Some(Value::Map(entries)) = rows[0].get_by_name("m") {
    for (key, value) in entries {
        println!("{key} = {value}"); // k = 1
    }
}

docs.title: Rust UDFs via WebAssembly
docs.text:
Run Rust user-defined functions on Spark, distributed on the executors, with no server-side plugin. You write plain Rust functions; the toolchain compiles them to WebAssembly, embeds the module, and ships it inside a standard Spark PythonUDF. The executors need only the wasmtime Python package - no Rust toolchain server-side.

Opt-in

This is behind the wasm-udf feature. Users who don't run Rust UDFs pull none of the extra dependencies and need none of the preconditions below.

docs.title: Write plain Rust functions
docs.text:
Annotate a module of functions with #[spark_wasm_udf]. For each function the macro infers the Spark signature from the Rust types, exports it to WASM, and generates a constructor under udf:: - a direct call udf::<name>(col0, col1, ...) (one column per argument, arity checked at compile time) that returns the result Column. A one-line build.rs compiles the module.

// src/main.rs
use spark_connect_macros::spark_wasm_udf;

#[spark_wasm_udf]
mod udfs {
    pub fn add_one(x: i64) -> i64 { x + 1 }                          // (Long) -> Long
    pub fn shout(s: String) -> String { format!("{}!", s.to_uppercase()) }
    pub fn sum(xs: Vec<i64>) -> i64 { xs.iter().sum() }              // ArrayType arg
    pub fn double_or_null(x: Option<i64>) -> Option<i64> { x.map(|v| v * 2) }
}

#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    use spark_connect::functions::col;
    use spark_connect::SparkSessionBuilder;

    let spark = SparkSessionBuilder::default()
        .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
        .get_or_create()?;

    // Pass columns straight in - one per argument. Signatures are inferred and
    // the compiled module is embedded; there is no `.wasm` file to load.
    spark
        .range(5)?
        .select([
            col("id"),
            udf::add_one(col("id"))?.alias("plus_one"),
        ])
        .show(20)?;
    Ok(())
}

// build.rs
fn main() {
    spark_connect_build::embed_wasm_udf("src/main.rs");
}

# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
spark-connect-macros = { package = "apache-spark-connect-macros", version = "4.3" }

# host-only: the client is not pulled into the wasm build
[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dependencies]
spark-connect = { package = "apache-spark-connect", version = "4.3", features = ["wasm-udf"] }

[build-dependencies]
spark-connect-build  = { package = "apache-spark-connect-build",  version = "4.3" }
spark-connect-macros = { package = "apache-spark-connect-macros", version = "4.3" }

Run it:

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown            # once
cargo run

Runnable examples

See examples/wasm-udf-inline/ (the UDFs and client in one file) and examples/wasm-udfs/ + examples/src/wasm_udf_macro.rs (UDFs as a reusable crate, called as wasm_udfs::udf::add_one(col("id"))?).

docs.title: Supported types
docs.text:
Arguments and results cross the WASM boundary in a binary ABI (spark_connect::wasm_udf::AbiType), inferred from the Rust signature:

Rust Spark SQL type i32 IntegerType i64 LongType f32 FloatType f64 DoubleType bool BooleanType String StringType Vec<u8> BinaryType Vec<T> ArrayType (of T) Option<T> nullable T

These nest arbitrarily - e.g. Vec<Option<String>> -> ArrayType(StringType, nullable).

A UDF whose arguments and result are all scalars, String, Vec<u8>, or one Option of those is sent as a scalar Arrow UDF and called once per Arrow batch; any other UDF is called once per row.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
build time   build.rs -> embed_wasm_udf() recompiles the source for wasm32
             (host-only code is cfg'd out) and embeds the .wasm module.

client       udf::add_one(col) builds a standard PythonUDF: a tiny Python runner
             plus the module are cloudpickled by value, so executors need only
             `wasmtime` - nothing to pre-deploy.

executors    the Python worker instantiates the module with wasmtime and invokes
             the exported entrypoint once per Arrow batch, or once per input row
             for signatures with arrays or nested Options.

The user never writes WASM, never touches the ABI, and never loads a .wasm file - they write add_one(x: i64) -> i64 and call udf::add_one(col("id")).

docs.title: Preconditions (only when using Rust UDFs)
docs.text:
Nothing here is needed unless the wasm-udf feature is enabled:

  • Build machine - the wasm32-unknown-unknown target (rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown), plus apache-spark-connect-macros and apache-spark-connect-build as (build-)dependencies.
  • Client (building the UDF command) - a Python interpreter with pyspark importable (used for its vendored cloudpickle and the pure-Python type parser). The packer script is embedded in the crate and run as python -c, so there is nothing extra to install or put on a path; point SPARK_CONNECT_PYTHON at the interpreter if it isn't your default python3.
  • Executors - the wasmtime Python package.
  • Spark - 4.3.0+.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
For non-deterministic UDFs or custom packer configuration, the macro also generates a builder udf::<name>_udf():

udf::add_one_udf()
    .as_nondeterministic()
    .call(vec![col("id")])?;

To call a UDF once per row instead of once per batch, set its eval type:

use spark_connect::udf::eval_type;

udf::add_one_udf()
    .with_eval_type(eval_type::SQL_ARROW_BATCHED_UDF)
    .call(vec![col("id")])?;

If you'd rather load a prebuilt module and spell out the types yourself, the lower-level factory mirrors pyspark.sql.functions.udf:

use spark_connect::wasm_udf::{udf, AbiType};

let wasm = std::fs::read("shout.wasm")?;
let shout = udf("shout", wasm, "shout", vec![AbiType::Str], AbiType::Str);
let c = shout.call(vec![col("name")])?;

docs.title: Which client am I using?
docs.text: pyspark-client-rust installs under the pyspark import name and mirrors the PySpark Spark Connect API exactly, so your code looks identical to code written for the reference client. That is the whole point of a drop-in - but it also means it is worth being deliberate about which client is installed, so that behavior and bug reports are attributed to the right project.

docs.title: The three packages on PyPI
docs.text:
Package Import What it is pyspark pyspark Full Apache Spark for Python - Spark Classic (JVM/py4j) and the Spark Connect client. pyspark-client pyspark The reference Spark Connect client: Connect-only, pure Python, gRPC via grpcio. pyspark-client-rust (this project) pyspark A Spark Connect client with the same API surface, backed by a native Rust engine (gRPC via tonic) instead of grpcio/py4j.

All three expose the pyspark package name, and only one can be installed into an environment at a time. pyspark-client-rust is a drop-in for pyspark-client: uninstall any existing pyspark / pyspark-client, install pyspark-client-rust, and your Spark Connect code runs unchanged (see Installation).

docs.title: Same API, different engine
docs.text:
What is the same: the Python API surface, the spark.connect protobuf protocol on the wire, and the results you get back. Plans built by this client are checked byte-for-byte against the reference client, and the official PySpark Connect test suite runs against it (see Compatibility).

What is different: the engine. The reference client builds protobuf plans, manages the gRPC channel, and decodes Arrow results in Python; pyspark-client-rust does all of that in Rust. That is where the performance difference comes from - biggest on client-bound work such as plan building and result decoding - and it is also why the two are separate implementations that can have separate bugs.

docs.title: How to tell, at runtime
docs.text:
Python attributeLog on connectpip 
import pyspark
pyspark.__rust_client__   # True only in pyspark-client-rust
pyspark.__engine__        # "rust"
pyspark.__version__       # the Spark version this client targets, e.g. "4.3.0"

The first time a session connects, the client emits a one-line INFO log on the pyspark logger:

pyspark-client-rust 4.3.0 active: Spark Connect client backed by the native Rust
engine (tonic), a drop-in for pyspark-client -- not the reference Python client.

Enable it with logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO).

$ pip show pyspark-client-rust

Switching back

Because all three packages share the pyspark import directory, uninstalling pyspark-client-rust alone leaves you without a working pyspark - reinstall pyspark-client (or pyspark) to switch back. See Installation for the exact steps.

docs.title: Reporting issues
docs.text: pyspark-client-rust is a separate implementation. If you hit a problem while using it, please file it against apache/spark-connect-rust (or the SPARK JIRA) rather than reporting it as a reference pyspark-client bug - confirm pyspark.__rust_client__ is True first. If a behavior differs from the reference client, that difference is itself the bug we want to hear about, since the goal is byte-for-byte parity.

docs.title: Server compatibility
docs.text: This client speaks to Apache Spark Connect servers 4.3.0 and later (see Compatibility). To talk to servers older than 4.3, keep using the reference client; the two can coexist in separate environments.
